title: Compiled Commentary on the Treatise on Response and Retribution (Volume Two)
excerpt: Regard the gains of others as your own gains; regard the losses of others as your own losses.

Two)
Translated and edited by the Liaofan Dharma Propagation Society
To be a good brother.
To rectify oneself and transform others.
To pity the orphan and compassion for the widow; to honour the aged and cherish the young.
Even insects and plants may not be injured.
One should pity the misfortunes of others, and rejoice in the goodness of others.
To relieve others in their urgency, and to save others in their peril.
To regard the gains of others as one's own gains, and the losses of others as one's own losses.
Not to publish the shortcomings of others, and not to parade one's own strong points.
To check evil and to promote good.
To give much and take little.
To bear insult without resentment.
To receive favour with surprise.
To bestow kindness without seeking repayment, and to give to others without afterwards regretting it.
Such a one is called a good man.
All men honour him; Heaven's Way protects him; fortune and emolument follow him; the hosts of evil stand far from him; and the spirits guard him.
Whatever he undertakes must succeed, and immortality may be hoped for.
He who seeks to be a celestial immortal should lay up thirteen hundred good deeds; he who seeks to be a terrestrial immortal should lay up three hundred good deeds.
To act unrighteously, and to walk contrary to reason.
To account wickedness an ability.
To bear to do deeds of cruelty and injury.
To work secretly against the good and the worthy.
To secretly deceive one's ruler and one's parents.
To be disrespectful to one's teacher.
To be false to the duties of one's office.
To deceive the ignorant and untaught.
To slander one's fellow students.
To be false, accusing, deceitful, and hypocritical.
To attack and expose the clan and the kindred.
To be hard and unbending, without benevolence.
To be fierce and perverse, following only one's own will.
To judge right and wrong improperly.
To set one's likings and dislikings perversely.
To oppress those below in order to win merit.
To flatter those above in order to win their favour.
To receive kindness without gratitude.
To brood over resentment without ceasing.
A Vernacular Condensed Edition of the Compiled Commentary, Exposition, and Evidential Cases on the Treatise on Response and Retribution, Volume Two
[Explanation]
He who is an elder brother must be affectionate towards his younger brothers; he who is a younger brother must be respectful towards his elder brothers.
[Analysis]

Brothers are as the hands and the feet. In the course of a whole life, there are only these few of them, and this too is the rarest thing in a human life! In the eyes of one's father and mother, brothers were originally one body! If some slight discord should arise between brothers, then the hearts of the parents will be troubled; and if the parents see the brothers loving one another as hand and foot, who knows how great their inward joy will be! Moreover, since brothers are called hands and feet, they share in one another's aches and itches, and should protect and support each other: how could there ever be a principle by which hands and feet should themselves disturb and fight one another? Therefore one should always remember: brothers are born of one and the same father and mother, and were originally one body! They are like bone and flesh, which is very hard to part! If one understands this principle, then even should brothers meet with some misunderstanding and quarrel, they will naturally be unable to bear quarrelling on; and as for wealth, they will naturally hold it light. The Chan Master Fazhao once made a verse, saying: “One breath, linked branches, each one flourishing on its own; let no idle word or two wound the heart. Each time we meet, each time we are older: how long can we remain brothers? Brothers dwelling together, forbearance brings peace; let no trifling thing give rise to strife. The children born before our eyes are brothers again: we leave them an example to look upon.”

The Precepts for the World of the Yuan Family says: “For a father to love his son, and an elder brother to love his younger brother: this is the duty proper to a father or an elder brother, and there is no need to insist that the son or the younger brother must be obedient in return. And so the son, or the younger brother, ought of himself to love his father and his elder brother; but neither need he insist that the father or the elder brother must of necessity be kind to him. If each only fulfils the duty that is properly his own, then the fault of each reproaching the other will naturally disappear. Moreover, one should strictly forbid servants and retainers to carry words between them, lest misunderstandings arise. And the words of a wife carry with them a greater or lesser share of feeling; though they be pleasant to the ear, let them not be listened to. Then words that estrange father and son, or brother and brother, will naturally cease; and even if such words exist, they will not avail.”

Master Wang Yangming once said: “The sage king Shun of antiquity could move the elephants to plough the fields for him, and the secret of it was simply that he did not look at the elephants' faults.” And so between flesh and blood we should speak only of affection, and not of reason; for to cling to reason is to wound affection, and to wound affection is itself unreasonable! With the Chengzi of the Song dynasty, a man once asked: “I serve my elder brother, and have already fulfilled all the principles of a younger brother, yet I cannot win my elder brother's gladness of heart: what then should I do?” Chengzi answered: “In serving your elder brother, you should keep reverence and affection in your heart, and must be utterly sincere and earnest; you may not harbour a sense of grievance and complain to others.” The man asked again: “Then how should an elder brother treat his younger brother?” Chengzi said: “An elder brother should be affectionate towards his younger brother: that is the principle proper to an elder brother.”
Story One:

In the Han dynasty there was a man named Tian Zhen, in whose household there were three brothers. Their father and mother had both already passed away, and so the three brothers discussed how to divide the property their parents had left behind into three equal shares, one share for each. Even the redbud tree growing in front of the hall of their house they decided to divide into three parts; and the very next day they were to set to work and cut the redbud tree into three. Strange to tell, just after the Tian Zhen brothers had so decided, this redbud tree suddenly withered. When Tian Zhen saw it, he was deeply shocked, and said to his two younger brothers: “The tree is of one stock, and hearing that it is to be cut into three, it has withered away! Can we men be less than a tree?” As Tian Zhen spoke, he could not hold back the sorrow rising in him, and wept; and for this reason the three brothers then decided not to divide the redbud tree. Strange to tell, as soon as the tree heard that the Tian Zhen brothers would not divide it, it came to life again. The three brothers were moved to understanding by this, and never divided their household again. From then on the brothers held their property in common and lived together in happiness; and their neighbours all praised them, saying: “The household of the Tian Zhen brothers is a gate of filial piety!” You must know that brothers are one of the heavenly relations, and are named together with father and son, husband and wife, as the Three Bonds; and so the ancients compared brothers to hands and feet, and hands and feet carry the meaning of never being parted from one another! For if they are parted they will be scattered, and if scattered they will be left alone, and being left alone they will presently come to extinction!
Story Two:

In the Song dynasty, Sima Guang, the prime minister, had an elder brother named Sima Kangbo who was already eighty years old. Sima Guang served his elder brother, serving him as he would have served a stern father; and again he cherished and tended him as though he were an infant. Each time they took a meal, after they had eaten a while, Sima Guang would ask: “Elder brother, you must eat your fill; otherwise you will go hungry!” And when the weather turned a little cold, he would stroke his brother's back and say: “Elder brother, are your clothes warm enough? Take care not to catch a chill!”
Story Three:

Zhou Wencan was by nature most affectionate towards his brother. His elder brother loved to drink, and depended upon Zhou Wencan for his living; once his elder brother, drunk, even beat Zhou Wencan. When the neighbours heard of it, they felt deeply aggrieved on his behalf, and scolded Zhou Wencan's elder brother, saying: “Your younger brother is so good to you: you eat his food, drink his drink, and live in his house; and when you are drunk you even beat him. As an elder brother, have you no conscience at all?” Yet Zhou Wencan angrily said to the neighbours: “My elder brother did not beat me at all! Why do you want to estrange the affection between us brothers?”
Story Four:

In the Song dynasty there were two brothers, Zheng Degui and Zheng Dezhang, both of a most affectionate and filial nature, who studied together and at night slept in the same place. Now Dezhang was upright and unbending by nature, and in his dealings with others was not sufficiently accommodating, and so he gave offence to an enemy; and this enemy devised a scheme to ruin Dezhang, who was thereupon sentenced by the authorities to death, and soldiers were soon to come to the house to arrest him. Degui knew that his younger brother had been ruined by another's plot, and felt exceedingly grieved; and he pretended to say to his younger brother: “They meant to ruin me in the first place; it has nothing to do with you! If I but go to the authorities and give myself up, then the truth will come out clearly; but if you go and surrender yourself to the authorities, you are as good as dead!” When Degui had finished speaking, he set out for the authorities to give himself up; and Dezhang ran after his elder brother, and the two brothers struggled with each other on the road, stamping their feet and holding their heads as they wept aloud; each striving to be the first to go to the authorities and die. Degui then quietly contrived to hinder and delay his younger brother from going to the authorities to be punished, and availed himself of the darkness of night to leave first. The next day Dezhang found that his elder brother was gone, and pursued him again, following him all the way to Guangling; by this time Degui had already died in prison. When Dezhang saw his elder brother's corpse, he wept so bitterly in his grief that he swooned away, four times in all. After Dezhang had cremated his elder brother's body, he carried his elder brother's ashes on his back and returned home to bury them; and he kept watch by his elder brother's grave for several years. Each time Dezhang wept most bitterly, the crows and many other birds would fly to his side and listen to him weeping, and would not even eat. Degui's children were very young, and Dezhang raised his elder brother's children with as much care as he raised his own.
Story Five:

In the period of the Wei, Jin, and Northern and Southern Dynasties, in Northern Qi there was a man named Puming, and between him and his brother there was a lawsuit over property that dragged on year after year; each of them moreover summoned witnesses to testify on his own behalf. At last a plaint was brought before Su Qiong, the governor of Qinghe. Governor Su summoned the two Puming brothers and admonished them, saying: “What is hard to obtain in this world is a brother; what is easy to obtain is land. Suppose you gain the land and lose the brother: how will your hearts feel?” As Governor Su spoke, tears fell from his eyes; and when the witnesses standing by saw it, there was not one of them who was not moved to tears by the governor's sincerity. The Puming brothers thereupon knocked their heads on the ground before each other and acknowledged their fault, each yielding to the other, and never again did they contend over property or go to law.
Story Six:

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: “In Huaiyin there was an official who had two sons, and from childhood the two brothers were at odds, so that in a whole year they would not meet even once. Later, when the elder brother lay gravely ill, he sent someone to call his younger brother to his sickbed, and holding his hand he said to him: ‘I married at nineteen, and in my youth I never won my wife's love; by the time I was thirty-eight my father and mother had passed away, and so in my later years I had no parents' love either. The longest companions of my life have been we two brothers alone; yet all our lives the two of us have been at odds, and only today do I begin to feel regret and to awake. But my life is already nearly over!’” When men hear what this dying elder brother said to his younger brother, those who hear it too should surely be moved!
Story Seven:

Zhang Shixuan lived in the period of the Five Dynasties. His father and mother had passed away while he was still young; and when he had grown up, of all his elders only one uncle remained. Now this uncle had seven sons, and one day the uncle said to Zhang Shixuan: “You have now grown to manhood, and I ought to divide the family property into two, one share for you and one for me. Do you think such a division fair?” Zhang Shixuan said: “Uncle, I cannot bear that the seven sons of your household should have but one share of property among the seven of them. Uncle, you may divide the family property into eight shares!” The uncle insisted that he would not divide it so, and Zhang Shixuan likewise insisted that he would not divide it the other way. Zhang Shixuan was seventeen that year, and was recommended to go to the capital to sit for the examination, and some twenty-odd others were recommended to sit at the same time. There was then a physiognomist skilled in reading faces, who pointed at Zhang Shixuan and said: “The one who will come out first in the examination this year is this young man!” When those of his own generation heard it, they all hooted with laughter, and even argued against the physiognomist's words. The physiognomist said: “The matter of composing essays is not something I can understand; but this young man's whole face is filled with the aspect of one who has accumulated great hidden virtue. This must be because he has done some great good deed, and that is why I dare to conclude that he will certainly come out first in the examination this year!” And indeed Zhang Shixuan passed as first in the examination.
[Further Analysis]

Nowadays there are truly far too many people who contend over property without any regard for the deep affection of brothers! It is so even between brothers born of the same parents, and how much the worse between brothers of the same father but different mothers! And when it comes to dividing property between cousins, then the ties of near and distant kinship grow more and more remote with every division! Who can be like Zhang Shixuan? The ancients said: “To treat one's brothers meanly is to treat one's parents meanly! To treat one's cousins meanly is to treat one's ancestors meanly!” For if the root of a tree suffers injury, then its branches and leaves must surely come to harm! This principle of tracing things back to their source is one that everyone should ponder three times!
[Conclusion]

The retribution of blessing or calamity that comes upon one who reverently complies with, or who deceives and opposes, his own brothers is ten times stronger than that which comes upon him for reverently complying with, or deceiving and opposing, other men! And the retribution of blessing or calamity that comes upon one for reverently serving and obeying, or for opposing and deceiving, his own father and mother is a hundredfold! Everyone should keep this principle firmly in mind and be vigilant over himself!
First one must rectify oneself, and further one must admonish and transform others, so that together we may cherish a good heart and together do good deeds.

As the saying goes, ‘to set others right one must first set oneself right,’ and ‘when one's own person is upright, things go well even without giving orders.’ Now if a man can rectify himself, there is nothing he cannot set right! For if a man can rectify his own conduct, everyone will respect him; and when a man understands the principle of reverence, that is the place in his heart where he may be transformed! If, at the place where this heart may be transformed, one uses a most sincere heart to move him gently, then naturally a single touch will set him turning, a single lift will bring him forth, and there will be none who does not accept and comply! But if I use my own rectitude to expose another's want of rectitude, then even though I reprove him but lightly, he will certainly not be willing to accept the teaching; and he will argue with me besides, contending over right and wrong, crooked and straight! This will instead destroy his good heart! This too is a common failing among those who love goodness today. Each time they admonish and transform others, they strike too heavily; and being obstinate and unable to adapt, they do not know how to use skilful means: this is truly a fault that should be cut off with all severity! Therefore, to rectify oneself one must first rectify the heart! For the heart is the master of the whole person and the root of all conduct. If the heart has no subtle awakening, delusive thoughts and emotional views will arise of themselves; and once delusive thoughts and emotional views have arisen, then the principle one perceives cannot be thoroughly and clearly understood, and right and wrong are thrown into confusion and turned upside down. Therefore in governing the heart one must seek subtle awakening; and after awakening, delusive thoughts and emotional cares all melt into the true heart! This is the method of rectifying the heart.

In the Song dynasty, Sima Guang was a man of loyal and generous nature and upright integrity, famed throughout the world. When he lived in Luoyang, the customs of Luoyang were all influenced and transformed by him, so that they changed entirely: there was no one who did not prize reputation and integrity, and all were ashamed to talk of wealth and advantage; everyone had a sense of honour and shame, knew to be vigilant, and did not dare to do wrong. Even young people of the younger generation who wished to do a thing would invariably remind and warn one another, saying: ‘Whatever you do, do not do evil! I fear that if Sima Guang comes to hear of it, it will go badly with us!’

In the Later Han there was a gentleman of rectitude named Chen Shi, who treated others with generosity and handled affairs with fairness. In his village, whenever anyone fell into a dispute, they would ask Chen Shi to decide who after all was right and who was wrong; and Chen Shi could always give an exact judgement, and would set out the reasons for right and wrong so that the parties were convinced in heart and had nothing to say. In time a proverb circulated in the village: ‘Rather be punished and beaten with the rod by the authorities than be named by Chen Shi and have your faults pointed out!’ One night a thief came to Chen Shi's house and hid himself on the great roof-beam of the house, where Chen Shi discovered him. Chen Shi rose from his bed, took up a candle, and called the young people of the household together to instruct them. Chen Shi said: ‘A man must not fail to urge himself on! A man who is not good is not necessarily evil by nature; it is only that he constantly does evil deeds, and once the habit is formed he cannot change, and so comes to this. Such a one is the gentleman up there on our roof-beam!’ When the thief heard Chen Shi's words, he was greatly startled, and jumped down from the roof-beam and acknowledged his fault and begged forgiveness before Chen Shi. Chen Shi admonished him with kindly words, bidding him resolve to reform and turn to goodness, and never again to follow a trade he would be ashamed to have seen. And he further gave him two bolts of silk, urging him to be sure to make up his mind firmly to reform. The influence of Chen Shi's way of doing things reached so far that it moved a whole county to transformation; and from that time on, there were no more cases of theft in the county.

In the period of the Five Dynasties, Fang Jingbo served as governor of Qinghe. Jingbo's mother was not only a woman of learning, but also most understanding of human feeling and thoroughly reasonable. In Beiqiu there was a woman who set out the facts of her son's unfilial conduct and brought a plaint to the governor's office; and Jingbo's mother said to Jingbo: ‘The common people are not yet able to understand principle or to comprehend propriety and righteousness, and they should not be reproved too severely!’ Thereupon Jingbo's mother summoned the Beiqiu woman who had accused her own son of unfiliality into the governor's residence, and ate together with her, and bade her son stand beside them and watch how Governor Jingbo waited upon his mother at table. Thus ten days passed, and the unfilial son said to his mother: ‘Mother! I was wrong. I will certainly reform and serve you with filial piety; let us go home!’ Jingbo's mother then said to Jingbo and to the Beiqiu woman: ‘Though this child has outwardly shown a look of shame, in his heart he has not yet truly felt shame!’ For this reason she kept the Beiqiu woman and her son in the governor's residence for more than twenty days longer. At this, the Beiqiu woman's son suddenly knelt before his mother and knocked his head on the ground in repentance, until his head bled; and the Beiqiu woman was so moved by this that her tears ran down her face, and she begged the governor to permit mother and son to go home. Later, the Beiqiu woman's son was indeed famed for his filial piety.

To take pity on and have compassion for orphans, and to do one's utmost to bring them up and educate them and to establish them in a lifelong calling; to relieve and succour widows, and to do one's utmost to protect them and to establish their lifelong chastity; to honour the aged, so that they obtain respect, support, and peace; and to cherish the young, so that they obtain nurture and protection.

Orphans and widows are among the misfortunes of human life; and if one becomes an orphan or a widow and is poor besides, that is worse still, and it is to be feared that even life itself can hardly be preserved! Therefore in bestowing kindness and favour, orphans and widows should be ranked as the foremost objects. The parents of an orphan, the husband of a widow: even in the unseen world they will feel gratitude without end! Old age and youth are stages that human life must necessarily pass through; and if at such a time one is poor and ill, that is the harder still, and it is to be feared that even survival is not easy! Therefore King Wen of Zhou, the sage king of antiquity, made but this the focus of his government: ‘Have compassion on these solitary ones’; and the aim of Confucius too was but to say: ‘The aged, let them be at peace; the young, let them be cherished.’ Why is this? The purpose is simply to make it easy for men's good hearts to come forth! Now there are truly too many good deeds to be done, and it is very hard to do them all perfectly. Those without means should of course do their own hearts' best and act according to their strength; but those with means should earnestly and solidly perform the work of compassion and relief, and warmly and truly accomplish the task of honouring the aged and cherishing the young. They may not say: ‘It is enough that I have the intention,’ for that is an irresponsible word of excuse!

In the Zhou dynasty, in the state of Lu there was a woman who, when the state of Qi attacked Lu, in the midst of the chaos of war threw away the infant she was carrying in her arms and took up instead the child she was leading by the hand. When the soldiers of Qi saw what this woman of Lu did, they thought it very strange, and asked her: ‘You threw away the child you were carrying in your arms: whose child is the one you threw away?’ The woman answered: ‘He is my own child!’ The Qi soldiers asked again: ‘Then whose is the child you are now carrying in your arms?’ The woman said: ‘He is my elder brother's child.’ The Qi soldiers pressed further: ‘Why did you cast away your own child and take up instead your elder brother's child?’ The woman answered: ‘A son is a private love to his mother; but a nephew is a public righteousness to his aunt. If I were to turn my back on public righteousness and lean to private love, then I would cut off the orphan left behind by my elder brother, and that is what I would not do!’ When the soldiers of Qi heard this woman's explanation, they said: ‘In the outskirts of Lu there are still women who hold to the principles of righteousness: how much more so the ruler of Lu!’ With that they withdrew their troops and returned to Qi, and attacked Lu no more. When the ruler of Lu heard of the matter, he bestowed many goods and valuables upon this woman, and gave her the title of the Righteous Aunt of Lu.

A woman of the state of Lu could give up a private love and keep alive her elder brother's orphan; and because of a single word of hers, the safety of the whole state of Lu was preserved and a war averted. Yet the so-called bearded men of today, when the state is in peril, instead turn their backs on righteousness and live on in dishonour: can they look upon the conduct of the Righteous Aunt of Lu without feeling shame?

When Yang Danian was twenty years old he passed as first in the imperial examination. He was a colleague of Zhou Han and Zhu Ang, and both Zhou Han and Zhu Ang were already very old; yet Yang Danian often belittled and insulted them. Zhou Han wished to admonish Yang Danian, saying: ‘Do not insult us because we are old: one day you too will be old!’ But Zhu Ang shook his head and said to Zhou Han: ‘Say nothing to him, say nothing to him! Lest we be insulted by him again!’ And indeed Yang Danian died in the prime of his manhood.

As the common saying goes, ‘Honour the aged, and you shall yourself grow old.’ One should know that the aged have long and wide experience, and to live to so great an age may be called long life; and long life is moreover the first of the Five Blessings! This is precisely what young people should be unable to emulate and reverence fast enough: how then can they treat the aged with contempt? Yet the people of the world, because the aged have dim eyes and the tottering bearing of age and are troubled in their movements, either dislike them or insult them: who is willing to revere and serve the aged with care? Seeing the example of Yang Danian, who insulted the aged and died young, I hope that young people who do not revere the aged may suddenly reform and repent, and cherish a generous heart. Whenever they meet an aged person, let them hold an equal mind: whether he be rich or noble, or poor and lowly, let them revere him equally; then they themselves will be able to live long in the future! Never insult the aged, for that will cut short your own blessings and your own span of life!

When Wang Bin was young he was much afflicted with illness, and his sickness was no light one. He thought to himself: ‘My body is so poor that I certainly cannot live long!’ From then on, whenever he saw an aged person he was most reverent towards him and moreover envied him. If an aged person passed by the gate of Wang Bin's house, though his station were poor and lowly, Wang Bin would invariably rise and salute him; and when Wang Bin walked abroad and met an aged person, he would invariably yield the path and let the aged person go first. Afterwards Wang Bin's illness gradually mended, his strength grew ever more robust, and he actually lived to the age of ninety-three.

In the Sui dynasty there was a monk who lived to be more than a hundred years old. He deeply understood the subtle and profound meaning of the Lotus Sutra, and once told the assembly: ‘This poor monk reveres the aged just as he reveres his own father and mother, and serves them just as he serves a bodhisattva. Whatever lay within my power to do, there was nothing I did not do with all my heart and all my strength. That this poor monk in this life can penetrate the Buddha-dharma and moreover has lived so long is all because of revering the aged! Therefore I hope that you will not treat the aged with contempt or insult, for that will diminish your blessings and cut short your years! You must know that fame and profit in this world are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, gone in the snapping of a finger; you must by all means awake, and not be bound fast by the fame and profit of the world. You should apply yourselves to the work of your own mind and nature; otherwise you will but have come to the human world for nothing, and will have let this precious human life pass by in vain! As for all that the Buddhas teach, ‘May my life be long, and may I diligently practise every good; may my blessings and virtue be abundant, and may I broadly benefit every being’ -- to miss all of that is truly a pity! If young people only know to rely on their own cleverness and to be proud of their talents, and treat the aged with contempt and insult, and do not know that long life is a blessing conferred by Heaven, and that the aged are the objects revered by the sage kings, then however great a young man's abilities may be, it is hard to say that he will live to be as old as they!’

In the Tang dynasty, Yuan Dexiu's family was exceedingly poor. His elder brother died young, leaving behind an infant not yet a full month old; and then his elder brother's wife, grieving to excess over her husband's death, died before long as well. The child was therefore left with no milk to drink and was like to starve to death. Yuan Dexiu wept and wailed day and night; and taking his elder brother's child in his arms, he let the child suck at his own breast. Strange to tell, ten days passed in this way, and milk actually flowed from Yuan Dexiu's breast; and the child, fed on Yuan Dexiu's milk, was able to survive and grow up. This matter, though it belongs to the accidental, shows plainly that to cherish the young truly accords with the heart of Heaven, and that is why such a response came about! Confucius said: ‘Cherish the young.’ Mencius likewise said: ‘Cherish my own young, and extend it to the young of others.’ These are the handed-down teachings of the sages and worthies, and those who are elders in a family should ponder them well!
Though they be tiny insects, or insensate plants and trees, they too may not be injured!

Here it is said that even the smallest insects and the grasses, flowers, and trees may not be injured; how much less then the heavier and greater lives besides! That people today injure living creatures at will is truly because they do not know that all living beings that move and have spirit are possessed of Buddha-nature! The Confucians too have the teaching that ‘when trees are growing, they may not be broken’: how then can one say that insects are merely tiny creatures, and that grasses and trees have no consciousness, and so injure them at will?

In the preface to the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment it is said: ‘Whatever has blood and breath must have consciousness; whatever has consciousness must be of one body!’ The Surangama Sutra likewise says: ‘The Tathagata constantly teaches that the myriad forms of the universe are all manifested by our own mind; that all causes and effects within and beyond the world, even the motes of dust of the world, are the results produced by this true mind; and that among them even a single blade of grass, a single leaf, a single thread, a single knot, if one traces them to their root, in truth all have their own nature!’

Again, for example, the Dharma Master Dao Sheng preached the Dharma to the stones, and the stones nodded their heads when they heard it! How then can it be said of walls and tiles that they have no Dharma-nature? Again, for example, the redbud tree planted in front of the hall of the Tian Zhen brothers' house, when it heard that the three Tian Zhen brothers were dividing the family property and meant to cut it into three parts as well, at once withered; and thereby the three Tian Zhen brothers were moved to resolve never again to divide their household or their tree, and the redbud tree, hearing this, at once came to life again. How then can it be said that grasses and trees are without consciousness?
The meaning of the Exalted One's admonition here is that people should cultivate a heart of compassion towards all living beings and all insensate life alike.

Formerly, when the Buddha was preaching the Dharma, there was a clam in a nearby pond that leapt out of the pond in great joy and listened with a single mind by the edge of the pond to the Buddha preaching the Dharma. It happened by chance that this clam was pierced to death by the staff of one of those who had come to hear the Buddha's teaching; and because it had listened to the Buddha-dharma with a single mind, its merit was very great, so that after this clam died it rose to the Trayastrimsa Heaven and became the king of that heaven (that is, the Jade Emperor, whom Westerners call God). And from the Trayastrimsa Heaven it came again to the place where the Buddha was preaching, to listen to the Buddha expound the subtle meaning of the Dharma; and thereby it awakened and attained the fruit of srotaapanna, that is, the first fruit of the hearers. A clam is a very small creature, yet it afterwards attained a very high station. Judged by this case, even the tiniest insects may not be injured!

Formerly there was a monk who, in his cultivation, had not attained any fruit, and so received in vain the offerings of the Jingde father and son. After this monk died, he became a kind of plant called the straw mushroom in the garden of the Jingde household, providing vegetables for the Jingde household's food each day. If anyone else wished to take it for food, take it how they might, they could never get it. Now the straw mushroom is a most tiny fungus, yet it had this special connection; and judged by this case, even insensate grasses and trees may not be injured!

In Hangzhou there was a woman of extremely fierce temper. Whenever she saw ants walking beside the kitchen stove, she would burn them with fire, and no one knows how many ants she destroyed like this. She also often filled up the burrows of earthworms with quicklime. She had just borne a son who was still nursing, when one day she went out on an errand and returned home to find a great black mass upon the bed. In alarm she looked closely, only to discover that it was her own son, who had been bitten to death alive by a huge swarm of ants. The woman was heartbroken, and before long she too suddenly died a sudden death.

In Taicang Prefecture there was a man named Wu Yi. One night he dreamed that two burly men dressed all in green were begging him for help. When Wu Yi awoke he said to himself: “There must be something about to be killed!” When it was light he went out to investigate, and saw several men holding axes and saws, about to fell two ginkgo trees they had just purchased. Only then did Wu Yi understand the dream of the night before. He immediately brought out money and bought the two ginkgo trees, and so those two ginkgo trees were spared from being cut down!

The cruel-hearted, who constantly do evil, bring calamity upon themselves; one should pity them, admonish them, and transform them, so that they can turn from evil to good and transform calamity into blessing. The kind-hearted, who constantly do good, bring blessings upon themselves; one should rejoice for them and praise them, encourage them and help them succeed, so that they may practice good all the more and their blessings be boundless!

Mr. He Longtu said: “When a person first begins to do evil, it is only because of a single mistaken thought at that moment — it is not that he cannot be dissuaded or stopped! Even after he has done evil, there still remains a single thought that his conscience is not yet extinguished, and it is not that he cannot be saved! The world often rejects those who have done evil as if they were enemies; though they wish to wash their hearts and reform and become new persons, because they are not accepted by others, it is hard for them to find the courage to change!”

Everyone wishes to gain the merit of doing good, yet people vainly discriminate and calculate. The more talented only wish the good deeds to be done by themselves, while the more lowly do not wish the good deeds to be done all by others; some even invent falsehoods to wreck the good deeds of others. This only spoils their own state of mind, and does no harm to others at all. Little do they know that if others have good thoughts and good deeds, and I can inspire them, urge them, and praise them, so that they do them more perfectly and more completely, then the good of others is my own good as well — and this is merit without limit!

To go from the common to the holy, the gate of all good is, above all, to rouse the bodhi mind, which is the most excellent and the first. The bodhi mind is like a seed, because it can give rise to all dharmas of goodness. It is like good farmland, because it can cause living beings to grow in goodness. It is like pure water, because it can wash away all the afflictions in the minds of living beings. It is like a blazing great fire, because it can burn away all wrong views. The Nirvana Sutra says: “The Buddha said that cultivating a single good mind can destroy a hundred kinds of evil deeds, just as a very small fire can burn away everything! Know that the myriad good deeds all arise from a single thought of delight in goodness; when the whole virtuous mind is present, then is accomplished our perfect bodhi of eternal joy and the wondrous fruit.”

One night Yu Lingyi caught a thief at his home; the thief turned out to be the son of a neighbor. Yu Lingyi said to him: “It is because poverty has driven you that you have become a thief! I will now give you ten thousand cash as capital to help you earn a living; from now on, never do evil again!” The thief was just leaving with the money when Yu Lingyi called him back and said: “You are a poor man carrying much money home late at night; you may well be questioned by the night patrol. Better that you remain at my house and go home after dawn.” Yu Lingyi never spoke of this matter to anyone for the whole of his life. Later his descendants all passed the imperial examinations in succession; everyone said this was the retribution of one who pitied, admonished, and transformed an evil person.

In the Later Han there was a man named Pang Tong, who whenever he praised the good deeds and good conduct of others always exaggerated beyond the truth. People found this strange and asked him why. Pang Tong replied: “In the present age good people are few and evil people many. To improve the corrupt customs of society and increase one’s own progress in the Way, if I do not praise the good deeds of others to the fullest, then those who wish to do good will be even fewer! When you praise ten people, five may err, but five do not err; and in this way those inclined to do good may all the more spur themselves on — and that suffices!” The instruction of Lord Guan once said: “May heaven forever give birth to good people, may people forever do good deeds, may mouths forever speak good words.” Mr. Pang Tong may be said to have understood this instruction well and to have practiced it himself; he is truly of benefit to the world and to the human heart!

When one meets the urgent needs of others — as in sickness the urgent need of medicine, in death the urgent need of burial, in hunger and cold the urgent need of clothing and food, and so forth — we should generously open our purses and give help in time to meet the urgent need. When one meets the calamities of others — such as floods, fires, accidents, the ruin of families, and the like — we should, according to our own strength, go to rescue and remove their perils, so that they may turn danger into safety.

When others meet with calamity and distress, if one can make good use of a single word to rescue them, this merit can, above, benefit one’s ancestors, and, below, bring blessings to one’s children and grandchildren. Know that the same hand that pushes a person down also lifts him up! The same mouth that harms others also praises them! Therefore one would rather use the hand that lifts than open the mouth that harms. If one can act accordingly, one need not ask about the future — the future will surely be good!

The Record of Auspicious Blessings says: “Whenever one saves a life, the expense to oneself is not great; only those well-fed and well-clothed, who do not know the suffering of hunger and cold, think it of no account and pay no attention. When the faces of the starving turn sallow and green, one neither heeds nor cares; when the starving are gravely ill and in danger, one thinks it now hopeless to save them, and so watches them die before one’s eyes. Even if a well-meaning person passes by and sees, he can only heave a sigh of sympathy; while the other passers-by look askance, unconcerned, and keep far away.”

Know that a hungry person easily falls ill; once ill he has no strength to beg, and so the more he hungers the deeper and more serious it grows. Thus the earlier the starving are rescued the better. At the very start, only three or four liters of grain are enough to restore their strength and vitality. For a rich man, the cost of a single night’s lodging is enough to save ten lives! If the strength of many is gathered together, it is done even more easily. For instance, one may set up an empty room, pile up straw or warm clothing in it, and take in these poor, sick, cold and hungry people, so that they need not endure in the open the suffering of wind and dew and sleeping out of doors; in this way they can more easily nurse their bodies and recover their health, especially in cold weather, where the need is most urgent! Such measures for rescue can prevent many of the starving from falling ill or dying. For when a person falls ill and no one pays heed, one added disease comes upon him; if he still stays outside and is drenched by the rain, a second disease is added; with the added fear and anxiety, a third disease; and with an empty stomach and nothing to eat, filthy clothing, and wandering and dragging on, how can there be any hope of living! Therefore we should put ourselves in their place and think for them: all are human; if we, like them, met with calamity, we should be just as they are now! Today, happily lacking neither food nor clothing, one wishes instead to increase one’s own pleasures, hoping to store up more wealth for one’s descendants to enjoy; and yet before the pressing good deed of saving those before him, he parts with no coin at all. Little does he know that flood, fire, thieves, sickness, and calamity — these can all sweep his family wealth away! Know that the blessings we now enjoy were formed by doing good and giving in past lives, and are by no means amassed through meanness and stingy scrimping! Once impermanence arrives, when the eyes close and the legs stretch out, nothing can be carried away; what wealth is left becomes only the means of descendants’ wine, women, and gambling! Better to accumulate virtue and leave a blessing to posterity — this is truly a reasonable man! To regard money as one’s life and refuse to part with a single coin is truly to be without a mind and without wisdom!

In the Song dynasty, Wang Zeng, on his way to the capital for the examinations, heard a mother and daughter weeping by the roadside, their weeping most grievous. Wang Zeng asked a neighbor in the area, who said: “This mother and daughter are poor and have fallen into arrears with the public treasury, and the officials press them hard; so they are about to sell the daughter to repay the debt — that is why they weep.” Wang Zeng then went to visit their home and found it was truly so. Wang Zeng said to the mother: “You may sell the daughter to me. Because I hold office, I must often pass through this place, and so mother and daughter may see one another often.” Thereupon he gave her the amount of money she owed the treasury, and agreed that after three days he would take the daughter away. But after three days, Wang Zeng did not come to take the daughter. The mother found it strange and went to the place where Wang Zeng was staying; but Wang Zeng had already departed, and had left behind a letter telling the mother to choose a faithful and dependable family for her daughter to be married into. Later, when Wang Zeng went to the capital for the examinations, he was ranked first three times in succession, attained a very high office, and was even enfeoffed by the emperor as the Duke of Yi.

In the place called Xinjian there had once been a great famine. A certain family was reduced to the utmost poverty, leaving only a little more than a liter of grain. So they cooked rice and put poison in it, intending to eat their fill together and then die. Just as they were about to eat, the village headman happened to arrive to press them for the arrears they owed the public treasury; seeing their cooked rice, he wanted to eat it. The poor man hurriedly stopped him, saying: “This rice is not what you should eat!” and then tearfully told him the reason. The headman was grieved on hearing it, and said to him: “How can your family have come to such poverty! Though my family also lacks grain, we still have five pecks of rice. Let it be so — come home with me and take some rice, and at least you can eat for a few more days!” When the poor man carried the rice home, he discovered fifty taels of gold inside the rice bag. Thinking this must be public money, he hurriedly took it back to return it to the headman. The headman said: “This is not the government’s money; it must be heaven’s gift to us!” So they divided the gold equally, and both families were able to pass through the famine year in safety.

The man Duan Nianba had grain stored in dozens of granaries. When a famine year came, he wished to seize the chance to reap a windfall, and so raised the price of the grain to sell it. The authorities sent a man to Duan Nianba’s home to borrow grain for famine relief, and Duan Nianba agreed. But the next morning, on seeing a great crowd of starving people lined up outside his gate waiting for grain, Duan Nianba repented and would not give out the grain. The starving people then set up an uproar. Duan Nianba ordered his household to shut all the doors and turn everyone away. Just at that moment, suddenly the weather changed: great wind and rain, thunder and lightning, came together. Strange to say, the grain in the Duan family granaries all piled up, heap upon heap, out in the street. When the starving people saw it, they all hastened to seize it, and within less than a moment they had taken all the grain away; while Duan Nianba was struck dead by the thunder.
Supplementary Note

When a famine year comes, those who live near the mountains may gather pine and cypress to relieve hunger. The Records of Natural Studies says: “In a famine year, with nothing to eat, one may pound pine and cypress; the juice that is pressed out, taken together with boiling water, may be drunk until one is merely not hungry. Using the clear congee broth to take the pine and cypress juice is even better. Each time use five measures of pine juice and three measures of cypress juice, ground and taken; or one may use pine leaves alone, which is also fine; but one must abstain from all food, and then it will naturally have the effect of relieving hunger and curing illness.”

In Gaoyou there was a man called Zhang Baihu. Once, sitting in a boat, he saw a person far off clinging to the overturned hull of a boat, bobbing up and down in the utmost danger, crying loudly for help. Zhang Baihu called out, asking the fishing boats to go to his rescue, but none of the boats responded. Zhang immediately took out ten taels of silver and gave them to the boatman, who then consented to go to the rescue. Having saved the man, this one who was nearly drowned turned out to be none other than Zhang Baihu’s own son!

When one sees others fortunate and elated, one should feel as if it were one’s own fortune, and moreover do one’s utmost to support them; when one sees others unfortunate and dejected, one should feel as if it were one’s own misfortune, and should go to their rescue in every way.

People today, when they see the gain and loss of others, cannot take them as their own gain and loss. The reason is nothing but a single heart set on themselves. Hoping to gain and fearing to lose, they then give rise to the thought of fearing that others may gain and preferring to let others lose. At first it is only for one’s own profit, but gradually it comes to the point of harming others. Yet to envy the success of others and delight in their failure is in fact quite unrelated to success or failure in human affairs; it only spoils one’s own state of mind and plants the seed of evil, and in the end brings harm to oneself. Little do we know that the work of sages and saints is originally to eliminate the view of self, and that the insight of the enlightened must also break through vulgar feelings. If one realizes that self and others are originally one, and that gain and loss are all determined by heaven, then seeing the gain of others, one not only does not envy it but extends every kind of support and assistance; seeing the loss of others, one not only does not rejoice but gives every kind of rescue and protection — this is the true benefit for oneself!
Story:

When Xue Yuan was prime minister of the state of Yan, he could not treat people and handle affairs with an impartial heart, but envied what others gained and delighted in what others lost; he would not recommend worthy and able persons to Yan, but was envious of them and obstructed them, so that they could not be of use to the king of Yan. As a result, one of Xue Yuan’s sons died in prison, and all his other sons became cripples. Gongming Zigao then transmitted the Zhong Jing Jing (Sutra of the Middle Admonitions) to Xue Yuan; after reading the sutra and hearing the Dharma, Xue Yuan deeply regretted his past conduct, and made a vow to uphold and practice the teachings of the Zhong Jing Jing. In the end he preserved only a single child.
Fine Words:

Master Lianchi of the Ming dynasty once said: “As for people’s response to the temptations of wealth, sex, fame, and profit in this world, each person’s power of concentration in resisting such temptations differs greatly; now I will use a metaphor to explain it. Suppose here is a pile of fire, and beside the fire are set five different substances. The first is like dry grass: as soon as it touches the fire, it burns. The second is like wood: with only a breath of wind upon it, it too catches fire and burns. The third is like iron: it will not burn, but once the fire burns long enough it melts. The fourth is like water: not only does it refuse to burn, it even puts out the fire; but if the water is placed in a pot and heated, it is still brought to a boil by the fire! The fifth is like empty space: know that in empty space there is nothing to burn; however the fire may burn, it remains as still and unmoved as empty space! And as the fire burns on and on, after it has burned long enough it goes out of itself!” So those who would make the mind impartial should contemplate in this way.
Do not publicize the faults of others; rather, one should earnestly conceal them for him. Do not vaunt your own strengths; rather, keep them hidden and nurture your virtue.

When one hears or sees the faults of others, it is like hearing the names of one’s parents: the ears may hear them, but the mouth cannot speak them. Yet while the mouth surely cannot speak them, if the ears also would not hear them, would that not be even better! For who has no faults? If one publicizes the faults of others, the word inevitably spreads abroad, lessening their reputation and corrupting their conduct — for whose sin is this to answer! Unless one is an utterly unscrupulous scoundrel, one surely would not do such a thing.

One’s own virtues and strengths should be like those of a wise merchant, who keeps his wealth deeply hidden and does not reveal it; if the wealth is revealed, there is danger! In this life, every person surely has his strengths and merits; the most important thing is to know how to keep them veiled and nurture virtue, day by day renewing, and only then can one’s own character be accomplished. Laozi said: “Those who possess great virtue often appear, in their countenance, to look dull and foolish.” Zisi also said in the Doctrine of the Mean: “The gentleman’s way of conduct is to show nothing outwardly while the beauty is within; in time it naturally becomes evident day by day.” These teachers’ instructions are so clear and plain; therefore we should all carefully reflect on them!

In the Spring and Autumn period, King Zhuang of Chu one evening invited his ministers to a banquet. In the midst of the banquet the candles suddenly went out. A minister, drunk, took advantage of the darkness and tugged at the clothing of the king’s beloved consort, taking the opportunity to make advances. The consort at once tore off the minister’s hatband as evidence, and reported it to King Zhuang. On hearing this, King Zhuang said: “My purpose in feasting my ministers is that they all may drink to the full. Now one of them, drunk, has committed a fault. If, in order to make prominent my consort’s chastity, I would expose a minister’s fault, this is a thing I will never do!” So King Zhuang ordered his attendants not to light the candles, and sent word: “He who drinks with me — if he does not tear off his own hatband, it shows he has not enjoyed himself this evening!” When the ministers heard this, they all tore off their hatbands, and the banquet ended in great joy. Later, when King Zhuang fought with the army of Jin, he was closely besieged by the Jin forces; the battle was fierce and the situation most perilous. Then King Zhuang saw a warrior who, unafraid of death, fought his way forward against the Jin army, and by doing so freed the king from the crisis of being surrounded. When King Zhuang asked about him, he learned that this warrior was Jiang Xiong — the very minister whose hatband had been torn off by the consort that night while he was drunk!

Mr. Zhang Gongchen said: “Do not lightly discard the good of others; do not lightly believe the words of others; do not lightly follow the pleasure of others; do not lightly speak of the faults of others.” These are the ways of holding oneself in loyalty and generosity; and to reveal the faults of others is especially the very root of cruelty and treachery.

In the Song dynasty, Ouyang Xiu wrote extremely well and was a famous great writer in history; yet in receiving guests he always spoke much of the affairs of state administration and never spoke of literature. Cai Xiang, on the other hand, was expert in government affairs, yet in receiving guests he spoke much of literature and never of politics. Both gentlemen were excellent at keeping themselves veiled, and did not parade their strengths before others; therefore in history both enjoyed great renown, and they both rose to offices of the utmost eminence.

In the Yongchun era of the Tang dynasty, Lu Zhaolin, Luo Binwang, Wang Bo, and Yang Jiong — the four famous literati, known in history as the Four Outstanding Figures of the Early Tang — all enjoyed great renown for their writings. People at the time considered the four to have talent surpassing the age, and that, being young, they must surely reach the most exalted positions in future official life. But when Pei Xingjian saw the four, he said: “If a scholar is to prosper far and make great plans, one should first look to see whether he has a broad and generous capacity of character, and only afterwards at his writing! As for the four like Wang Bo, though their writing is good, they are in general hasty and shallow, fond of showing off their talent — this is not the stock that enjoys rank and fortune! Yang Jiong is a little the more calm and reserved; for him to come to a good end would be extremely fortunate!” Later the fates of the four indeed matched Pei Xingjian’s words. Lu Zhaolin, Wang Bo, and Luo Binwang all died young; only Yang Jiong lived the longer.

So from these facts one can see that ability is not equal to learning, vigor is not equal to virtue and capacity, and writing is not equal to conduct. People of old long ago clearly set forth this principle; therefore to show off one’s strengths is something a gentleman does not do! Especially the people of today, who often keep the phrase “worthy of pride” on their lips, and everyone hearing it takes it as a matter of course and does not regard it as wrong. Know that fullness attracts loss while modesty gains benefit; only the humble can truly enjoy blessings!

We should check people from doing evil, lest they gradually run wild and others come to be harmed by them; and, further, we should praise the good conduct of others, so that they may practice good without weariness and others also be guided by them.

As for a person’s doing evil, it is not caused by his original nature! But if a person is accustomed to doing evil and has been soiled too deeply, then he is hard to save. Whether one knowingly does wrong, or unknowingly acts in error, in the end one commits a sin that covers heaven. Trace it back to its beginning, and it is but a single mistaken thought at the start! Yet everyone has a conscience. When he first begins to err and the evil thought has just arisen, one should with earnest, kind words admonish him and remind him, and even do one’s utmost to stop him. Who has no heart? After such admonition and reminder, how could he fail to turn from evil to good? Even if, unhappily, one has already committed great evil, if I can reach him with perfect sincerity and curb him and stop him, then his good mind may well arise, and he may resolutely wash his heart, reform himself, and repent and wash away the evil karma he has committed! Moreover, people are not sages; how could they do good in everything! If he has but a single word or deed that is worthy, one should immediately praise him and commend him. This can make those already doing good firm in their resolve and the more diligent in doing good; and those not yet doing good, hearing of it, will also give rise to admiration and the resolve to emulate — is this not to obey heaven’s command?

The Daoists say: “Curb evil and promote good.” The Buddhists say: “Stop evil and practice good.” The Confucians say: “Conceal evil and promote good.” The doctrines of the three teachings seem to come from a single mouth. From this we know that the sage’s mind-substance is empty, spiritual, and clear to the very depths, and that not even the slightest trace of desire is retained! It is like a bright mirror reflecting things: as it is shone upon, so it manifests; and as it manifests, so it transforms away. Thus when the sage sees evil, he can naturally dissolve it; when he sees good, he can bring it to great brightness. Therefore the sage curbs evil and promotes good, solely in order to restore and complete the nature that living beings originally possess!

As the Four Teachings of Liaofan relates, before the great Shun became ruler, by the shore of Leize Lake he saw strong young fishermen all taking the deep places of the water to catch fish, while the old and weak fished where the current ran swift and the water was shallow. The strong young fishermen had taken for themselves all the good places. Seeing this, Shun grieved and pitied them. He thought of a method: he himself also went to catch fish; on seeing those who delighted in seizing, he covered over their faults and did not say anything of them; on seeing the more yielding fishermen, he praised them everywhere, took them as a model, and imitated their way of yielding. Thus, after Shun had fished for a year, everyone yielded the deep places, where fish were plentiful, to others. The story of Shun is only used to exhort people; one must not misunderstand it as urging people to catch fish. Know that catching fish is the sin of taking life, and must never be done. Then how is it that Shun, so clear and intelligent, could not have spoken a few pertinent words to teach the multitudes, and had to take part himself? Understand that Shun did not teach the people with words, but made himself the example, so that people on seeing it felt ashamed and changed their selfish minds — this is the careful effort of a person of deep purpose!

Curb your own evil, then you can curb the evil of others; promote the good of others, then you can urge others to do good.’ This means: first be able to curb your own evil, and then you can curb the evil of others; first be able to praise the good of others, and then you can urge others to practice good!

Whether brothers divide their property, or friends pass money between them, one should yield and make concession, giving the larger portion to the brother or friend and taking for oneself the smaller portion; let others have the advantage, while one is willing to take the loss.

Between brothers there is the bond of flesh and blood and the natural relationship of heaven, while wealth is a thing outside the body, and so one should surely yield! The Buddha said in the Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching: “Those of great desire, because they greedily seek after benefit, have more suffering and affliction than others; those of few desires, having nothing they seek and no greed, have not so much suffering and affliction. If a person wishes to free himself from all the various sufferings and afflictions, he should understand contentment; and the way of contentment is the most secure abode of wealth, honor, and happiness! The contented, even lying on the ground, are at ease and joyful; the discontented, even dwelling in heaven, are not contented and not joyful!” From this we know that if a person can, in matters of wealth, yield the more and take the less, his mind is naturally at peace; no external state can disturb it, and so he forever knows contentment and joy!

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: “Wealth is the vital breath of heaven and earth. A person in this world, without wealth, cannot survive; and there is no one under heaven who does not love wealth, and no day in which wealth is not used! Therefore wealth is an indispensable necessity of life. Yet the amount of wealth allotted to each person is fixed; to wish for more is impossible! However, each person’s habits in spending wealth are very different, and each has his bias: the prodigal flings away a thousand gold at a throw; the miser will not part with a single coin; the incorruptible, when a man sends him money at night, refuses it and will not accept; the greedy and tyrannical, even in broad daylight, will dare openly to rob and steal! Know that the miser’s insight is shallow and narrow, and he treasures each coin and cent as a precious thing; just as a bee protects the honey it has made, and a child protects the cake he hides in his breast, unwilling to share the least part with others. Yet this is still to keep what is his allotted share; it is merely annoying, and heaven does not on that account rage against his stinginess. But the greedy and tyrannical seek wealth that is not their allotted share, and are insatiable in greed; like a fish swallowing a boat, or a snake swallowing an elephant, in their greediness! Brothers quarreling, friends making enemies, robbers killing men, corrupt officials perverting the law, treacherous ministers betraying the state — all are produced by this single thought of greed! Therefore Taishang has in this chapter again and again set forth the calamity of coveting wealth. Yet to teach men not to wrongfully take wealth is right; if one were to teach men to take no wealth at all, that indeed would not do. So Taishang here gives the two words ‘more’ and ‘less’, enabling people to proportion themselves accordingly, as the proper way of taking wealth. And the measure of more and less has no fixed standard: for a poor man, one tael of gold is no small sum! For a rich man, ten thousand taels of gold are no great store! The incorruptible, who should receive a hundred coins but receives ten, does not feel it little; the greedy, who should receive a hundred coins but receives a thousand, does not feel it much. Only the man of impartial mind measures the amount he should receive, and in taking does not exceed his due portion — this is the method of taking less. Yet the human heart always fears having little and hopes for more, and this too is the common feeling of people. But if one can accord with conditions and not strive, then one naturally will not do evil; if one insists on always seeing more and withdrawing from it, would that not be to run counter to common feeling? Alas! Know that the coming of wealth has many different causes and conditions. The wealth we may take before our eyes is not necessarily what is allotted in our destiny; but in the hidden realm, all the number allotted to me I have no power to know, and no way to examine. If by any chance I take wealth that is not in my destiny, it is like taking poisoned wine and rotten meat to eat — can one eat it in peace and fullness? So better to withdraw from it, and that is the surer course! If I withdraw wealth that is not in my destiny, I can surely avoid my own fault; even if I mistakenly withdraw wealth that is in my destiny, then that withdrawn wealth will certainly come again from some other quarter! Faced with wealth, one must hold out and endure, and not let the eyes open at the sight of money and act carelessly! For the rich this is easier; for the poor it is far harder. If, knowing the difficulty, one still labors earnestly to do it, so that ghosts and spirits perceive this heart that dares not be in the least careless, then although one lives in the depth of poverty and hardship, one will not come to the point of being unable to go on living. If one can believe these principles truly and hold to them steadfastly, then the way of taking less is the way of becoming rich!”

In the Song dynasty there was a man named Xu Ji, who divided property with his second uncle. He first asked his second uncle to take all he wanted, and then he would take what was left. When the second uncle had finished taking, only a case of books and two run-down old rooms remained; Xu Ji accepted them with composure, and felt in his heart not the slightest resentment or regret!

In former times, in the district of Cixi, there were two scholars who were good friends. Later, the first scholar obtained a teaching post with a yearly salary of nine ounces of gold, while the second also obtained a teaching post, with a yearly salary of six ounces of gold. The first was delighted and said: “Next year neither of us will have any worries about making a living!” The second replied: “You, my elder brother, have only your wife at home, so nine ounces of gold is more than enough for your needs. But I have parents above me who must be provided for, so six ounces of gold is truly not enough!” Hearing this, the first scholar said: “Since you, my younger brother, are in difficulty, I will give my teaching post to you, and I will go and teach at the place where you were to teach!” After the first scholar arrived at the schoolhouse, he found beneath the bed a book already worn and torn, in which several prescriptions for external medicine had been copied out; the students said it had been left behind by the teacher who came before. When the winter holidays came and he returned home to rest, he saw several finely dressed servants who came to him in a fluster and asked: “Is there a physician of external medicine here?” And they said: “Our master is on his way from Fujian to Shandong to take up the post of provincial administrator, and on the road he was suddenly stricken with a boil on his back. The pain is unbearable, and he is very nearly dead. He has been in this state for almost three days now!” The scholar then recalled that prescription, which exactly suited this illness; and so he went with the servants to the place where the sick man lay, and there, following the prescription, applied moxa cautery. Sure enough, the provincial administrator’s back was healed. The administrator was overjoyed and brought out a hundred ounces of gold to reward him. The scholar then told the administrator how he had yielded his teaching post to his good friend, and how he had come by this prescription in consequence; and the administrator praised and commended him all the more greatly. It happened that the magistrate of Cixi was the administrator’s nephew, and he recommended the scholar with all his strength, so that the scholar was promoted and entered the county school as a stipendiary student.

Alas! Even blood brothers will contend over money and goods; how much more so friends? Because the first scholar could reflect that his friend was unable to provide for his parents, he gave up the greater and took the lesser, letting his friend take the greater. Know that although one or two ounces of gold is a small thing, this righteousness far exceeds the worth of a thousand carriages and horses! And so the scholar in the end gained both fame and profit, and all of it came from this single thought of yielding.

Though one suffers insult from others, one should only blame one’s own shallow virtue and scant merit, which cannot move others; and therefore one should all the more accumulate virtue and pile up merit, and never resent others.

Know that when you suffer insult from another, the only thing to do is at once to turn inward and ask whether you yourself were in the wrong. If you were, then the insult is entirely reasonable and you ought to accept it! If the fault lies with the other, then the insult ought not to have been given; yet even though it is aimed at you, it is still as though no insult had been given at all! Not only should you not resent it, there is truly nothing to resent! From ancient times, all who possessed great wisdom and great courage were certainly able to endure small shames and small resentments; only thus could they accomplish great deeds and achieve great merit. How could this be a principle that the narrow-minded and shallow-sighted could ever understand!

Mr. Yan Maoyou of the Ming dynasty was a native of Pinghu County in Zhejiang Province. He once instructed his sons and younger brothers, saying: “No one who has never undergone the discipline of practicing patience can ever know how difficult the word ‘endure’ truly is! And unless the two thoughts of good and evil are at war within the mind, one can never appreciate how wondrous the word ‘endure’ truly is! If a person cannot endure insult and bear hardship, then even though he has a good heart, the moment others provoke him it is gone, and the moment others frustrate him he falls away. Hence Mencius said: ‘When Heaven is about to confer a great office on a man, it will surely first temper his mind and purpose, causing him to discipline himself in the practice of steeling the mind and enduring his nature.’ This is precisely to make every person able to pass through this one barrier! Broadly speaking: in giving charity and relieving others, one need not mind incurring a little of others’ anger; in planning for others, one need not avoid others’ resentment and blame; one who takes on responsibilities must be able to bear resentment, and one who undertakes the work of exhortation and teaching must not avoid others’ mockery and criticism. If you set your heart on treating others generously, you will perhaps meet with their ridicule and insult; all such perversities will likewise follow along after good intentions and good deeds. If you cannot understand the principle at work in this, then you are not a person who can truly practice goodness!”

Fu Bi, a famous minister of the Song dynasty, instructed his sons and younger brothers, saying: “The word ‘endure’ is truly most subtle and wondrous! If a person, beyond being upright and frugal, adds to that the discipline of practicing this word ‘endure,’ then there is nothing he cannot accomplish!” When Fu Bi was young, someone reviled him, and a bystander said to Fu Bi: “Hey! Someone is reviling you!” Fu Bi replied: “He is probably reviling someone else.” The bystander said again: “He is naming names and pointing straight at you!” Fu Bi then said: “The world is so vast; is it possible that there is no one else with the same name and surname as mine? He is not reviling me!” When the man who had reviled Fu Bi heard this, he felt exceedingly ashamed.

Mr. Yan Guangzhong said: “The word ‘endure’ is the hardest of all! If a person can endure, then his moral character and breadth of mind must be great indeed; but by the time he can no longer endure, it is already his inner habit of arrogance and conceit overflowing! There is an old poem that says: ‘The youth who crawled beneath the legs of men bore no offense; the old man by the bridge was startled and resentful. If in life one does not look to the evening of one’s years, why should the Marquis of Huaiyin be reckoned less than Wencheng?’ This poem speaks exceedingly well. Han Xin, the great general of the Han dynasty, was able in his youth to endure the humiliation of crawling between another man’s legs, and thereby accomplished the earth-shaking great enterprise of his later years, being enfeoffed by Emperor Gaozu of Han as King of Qi. But after Han Xin had achieved fame and success, he grew smug and self-satisfied and could endure no more; in the end, because he had humiliated Marquis Jiang (Zhou Bo) and Fan Kuai, he was put to death. This is like drinking wine: once one has drunk to the full measure, one naturally can hold no more.

In former times, in the district of Jiangyin, there was a wealthy man surnamed Xia. One day, while he was playing chess with a guest, a man suddenly came running up shouting at the top of his voice, saying to him: “Xia! I owe your household no more than two ounces of silver in interest, so why have you ordered your people to come to my house every day to press me for repayment?” Before Mr. Xia could answer, the man began cursing furiously; and he even overturned the table, so that the chess pieces fell scattered all over the ground. Mr. Xia smiled and said: “The purpose of your coming to my house to tell me this is simply that you wish to be excused these two ounces of interest, is it not?” Thereupon he took up his brush and wrote out a document cancelling the two ounces of interest. The man took the document and hurried off, thanking him profusely. Mr. Xia’s guest, having witnessed this scene with his own eyes, admired him greatly and exclaimed in praise: “Mr. Xia, you are truly a gentleman of abundant virtue!” Mr. Xia said: “Endurance is the gate of all mysteries! In general, when dealing with the world and receiving people, if someone visits perversity upon me, it is like having walked into a thicket of thorns; at such a time I can only walk slowly and gently untangle the thorns that block my way, for how could those thorns make me angry? Or again, it is like an empty boat bumping into me, or a loose tile striking me; if I can keep my mind unmoved, then this resentment can be dissolved. Besides, this man’s face was fierce and his words violent, so he must have come prepared for something. I feared that if I provoked him, some unforeseen turn might occur, and so I simply excused him the interest.” That very evening word came that the man had died in the latrine of his own home. On close inquiry into the cause, it turned out that this man, driven to the end of his rope by debt collectors, had taken poison beforehand and come to Mr. Xia’s house intending to defraud him; but because he was grateful for Mr. Xia’s generosity in remitting his interest, he could not bring himself to do Mr. Xia harm, and so he hurried home in great haste to find the dung-green in the latrine to counteract the poison; yet it was already too late, for by then the poison had already broken out in full force and there was no time to neutralize it! When Mr. Xia heard this, he bowed in thanks to Heaven, and everyone accordingly came to respect and admire Mr. Xia.

Had Mr. Xia not cultivated himself well in ordinary times and cleared away the fire from his heart, how could he have held steady and endured at that critical juncture! And so, while enduring insult is certainly the key to cultivating the self, the secret of preserving wealth and honor is likewise to understand how to accept a loss!
Nirvāṇa

Sutra says: In former times there was a man who praised the Buddha’s appearance as a mark of great merit and blessing. Someone asked him: “How can you tell?” He said: “The Buddha was in the prime of life, yet the cultivation of his mind had already reached the point where the fire was purest blue; there was not the slightest trace of a fiery nature in his heart. Struck, he bore no hatred; reviled, he grew not angry. If this is not the mark of great merit and blessing, then what is?”

If people today could, when perversity stands before them, say: “Alas! He has come to perfect my mark of merit and blessing! I ought to feel exceedingly honored!” and could act thus, then though I am able to repay him, I do not stoop to reckon with him; and he too will be transformed and awakened by my generosity and forbearance!

Zheng Xuan said: “Be silent, be silent: boundless immortality is won from this. Yield, yield: a thousand calamities and ten thousand misfortunes vanish in a moment. Endure, endure: creditors and enemies hide themselves from this. Rest, rest: fame and merit that cover the world leave one unfree.”

Whenever one receives promotion, reward, or any such honor and favor, one should hold the thought that one is unequal to the burden, startled and fearful, fearing that one’s virtue is thin, one’s merit shallow, and one’s blessings insufficient to preserve them for long!

When a person receives honor and favor, even though it be what his own station deserves, he should still keep to his place and know contentment, and should feel as though startled by the favor. For “in fortune, disaster lies hidden,” as the ancients clearly taught! Ordinary people, as soon as blessings appear before them, forget themselves in their elation; and at that moment they have already planted the distant seeds of calamity. Moreover, when the sun reaches its zenith it begins slowly to decline; and after the moon is full it begins gradually to wane. This too is an unchanging principle. Therefore, after receiving honor and favor, one should all the more pile up merit and strive with all one’s might to repay, not daring the slightest slackness!
