King Cheng of Zhou enfeoffed Bo Qin, the son of the Duke of Zhou, with the state of Lu. The Duke of Zhou then warned Bo Qin, saying: “My son! His Majesty has enfeoffed you with the state of Lu; you must by no means grow proud on that account! I have heard that one whose virtue is vast and who can keep careful hold of reverence will certainly be able to preserve his glory for long; that one whose lands are broad and whose products are abundant, and who can keep careful hold of frugality, will certainly be safe; that one who occupies a high station and grasps great power, and who can keep careful hold of humility, will certainly be noble. A state whose people are many and whose arms are strong, and which can keep careful hold of awe and not invade its neighbors, will certainly be victorious. One of great intelligence and wisdom who can keep careful hold of the lesson that the greatest wisdom looks like foolishness will certainly gain great benefit. One of wide learning and much knowledge who can keep careful hold of the sense that his learning is still shallow will then have learning that is truly broad! These are what are called the six things to hold fast, and all of them are the virtue of humility. Know that the Way of Heaven, in all things, causes whoever is proud and self-satisfied to be diminished, while the humble are made to benefit. The Way of Earth, in all things, likewise causes whoever is proud and self-satisfied to be changed and not permitted to remain forever satisfied, while the humble are made moist and unfailing, as when water flows past a low place and must surely fill up its hollows. And the Way of Man is this: all men detest the proud and self-satisfied and love the humble! You must remember this well; do not, because you have been enfeoffed with the state of Lu, feel proud!” If a student can deeply comprehend the Duke of Zhou’s warning to Bo Qin, then the breath of arrogance in his own heart will have no way to arise; and if he should receive honor and favor, he will naturally have the feeling and thought of one startled by the favor.

When the Tang dynasty official Cen Wenben was appointed by the court to the office of Secretariat Director, he was not only not pleased but wore a sorrowful face. His mother saw this and asked him: “The court has given you weighty employment; why are you not pleased?” Wenben replied: “I am neither a founding elder and meritorious minister of the court, nor a relative of the imperial house, yet today I have undeservedly presumed upon the court’s honor and favor. Moreover, the Secretariat Director is an office of the very highest rank and the heaviest responsibility; that is why I feel sorrow and dread!” And to the guests who came to congratulate him, Cen Wenben said: “Today I accept only your condolences, and not your congratulations!”

Sima Guang of the Song dynasty wrote in a letter to his nephew: “Recently I have been favored by His Majesty’s grace with appointment as Vice Director of the Chancellery, and no small number of the civil and military officials throughout the court envy me! Yet I deal with them only with a dull and upright manner. I am like a yellow leaf tossed about in a fierce wind, and find it hard indeed to keep from falling! Therefore, ever since I received the appointment, I have felt only fear and no joy. You ought to understand my meaning!”

Not long after Lu Duoxun of the Song dynasty took up the office of Assistant Administrator, the clothing he wore and the comforts he enjoyed grew more and more extravagant by degrees. Lu Duoxun’s father saw this and said to him with a sorrowful face: “Our family has been a house of letters for generations and has always lived a plain and frugal life. Today you have suddenly become rich and noble, and your manner of living has turned so lavish and wasteful that you have long since forgotten what kind of days our family once lived.” Lu Duoxun did not take his father’s words to heart, but went on living a life of extravagance and waste; and in the end disaster came upon him and he failed.
In bestowing kindness upon others, never seek repayment; in giving goods to others, never regret it.

To bestow kindness on others and still hope for their repayment in return: this is one’s own greedy and clinging mind, not yet forgotten! To give goods to others and afterwards feel regret: this is one’s own stingy mind, not yet dissolved! Know that greed together with stinginess is what a gentleman will not do. The Diamond Sutra says: “A bodhisattva gives without clinging to any person, thing, or matter whatsoever.” It also says: “If a bodhisattva gives without clinging to appearances, his merit and blessing will be inconceivable!” From this we know that if a person can relieve and help others with goods and wealth, and can do so without inwardly perceiving a self that gives, outwardly perceiving a person who receives, and in between perceiving the goods that are given, this is called the three wheels are essentially empty, and is also called a single mind of purity. If one can give in this way, then though one gives no more than a bushel of rice, one may plant blessings that are boundless and without limit; and though one gives no more than a single coin, one may dissolve the offenses committed over a thousand kalpas. But if one has the slightest thought of hoping for repayment, then though one spends two hundred thousand ounces of gold to relieve others, one still cannot obtain perfect blessing! As for the two words “regret” and “remorse,” these above all mark the dividing line between sage and common person in a human life. If one feels remorse for evil deeds done, then the evil thoughts in one’s mind will gradually cease in the future. But if one feels regret for good deeds done, then the good thoughts in one’s mind will no longer arise in the future! If a person, after giving, still feels regret, then he would do better not to give and not to bestow at all; that would be the safer course!

If people of the world wish to fill their granaries with the five grains, and to lack for nothing year after year, then they must take the seed of rice and wheat, diligently work the plough, and sow that seed in the fields; for if they do not sow, the five grains in the granary will quickly be used up. The principle within the Dharma is just the same: take a mind of filial piety, a mind of compassion, and a mind of reverence as the seed; take clothing, food, wealth, and your own life as the ox and plough; take your father and mother, the poor and the sick, and the Three Treasures of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha as the field. If a Buddhist disciple wishes to obtain the hundred blessings and adornments within the storehouse consciousness, and blessings that shall not be exhausted life after life, he must with a mind of compassion, reverence, and filial piety reverently make offerings of clothing, food, and wealth, and even of his own life, to his father and mother, to the poor and the sick, and to the Three Treasures of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. This is called planting blessings; for if one does not plant blessings, one will be poor, lacking both blessing and wisdom, and will enter upon the perilous road of birth and death! The field of planting blessings spoken of here is like the field in which grain is planted; and therefore it is called the field of blessing.

Giving may be divided into three kinds: the giving of Dharma, the giving of wealth, and the giving of the mind. To exhort, teach, and transform others by all manner of skillful means is called the giving of Dharma, and the merit of the giving of Dharma is the greatest. The giving of wealth means using money and goods to relieve others. The giving of the mind means having no money to give in relief of the poor and destitute, yet in one’s heart pitying the other’s suffering and wishing to help though unable to help; this too may be called giving.

Li Shiqian, a man of the Sui dynasty, lost his father when he was small, and he served his mother with the greatest filial piety. By the time he was twelve, he had been given weighty employment by the Prince of Guangping of Wei and held the post of Adjutant of the Prefectural Office. His household gradually grew wealthy, and he brought out several thousand piculs of millet to lend to his fellow townsmen. Whenever a lean year or a poor harvest came, he would gather the townsmen who owed him grain, burn the IOUs on the spot, and say to them: “What you owed me has all been repaid; you owe nothing!” In the spring of the following year he again brought out seed and distributed it to the poor farmers to sow, and thereby kept many people alive. If anyone died, he would pay out money to help bury the dead. Someone praised Li Shiqian for accumulating hidden virtue, and Li Shiqian said: “Hidden virtue is like a ringing in the ears: only oneself can hear it and know it; others cannot hear or know it! Now that you already know of it, what hidden virtue is left to speak of?” One day Li Shiqian dreamed of a deity clad in purple who told him: “The Lord on High commends the abundance of hidden virtue you have accumulated, and will cause your descendants to flourish beyond all measure!”

Fan Zhongyan, prime minister of the Song dynasty, once sent his son Yaofu back to their home village in Suzhou to fetch five hundred hu of wheat. On the road Yaofu met an old friend, Shi Manqing, who said to him: “I have no money to pay for a funeral!” When Yaofu heard this, he at once gave Shi Manqing the five hundred hu of wheat, together with the boat that carried it. When he reached home he had not yet had time to speak of it when Fan Zhongyan asked him: “On this journey home, did you meet any old friends?” Yaofu replied: “I met Shi Manqing, and he is so poor that he has no money to pay for a funeral!” Fan Zhongyan said: “Why did you not give him the wheat and the boat that carried it?” Yaofu said: “Father, I have already given Shi Manqing both the wheat and the boat!”

From this we know how of one mind were father and son in the Fan household, and how greatly they loved to do good and to give! How unlike the people of today, who show reverence only to the rich and noble and do nothing but add flowers to brocade, yet will not relieve the poor and suffering or do the good work of sending coal in the snow. And even among those who are willing to give away a little wealth, is there anyone who gives without seeking repayment and does not regret it after giving?

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: “Even birds and beasts know how to repay kindness and requite goodness; how can a man, born a human being, fail to understand the principle of gratitude and repayment? What is most unbearable of all is the ‘look of virtue,’ that is, helping others while wearing on one’s face an expression that demands repayment. Once that ‘look of virtue’ appears, then the person I have helped and favored will feel ashamed and uneasy in his heart; and when that shame and unease have dissolved, resentment will arise next! In former times there was an official who had once saved a man’s life; afterwards the man he saved gradually grew wealthy, while this official gradually grew poor. It happened that the official passed by the house of the man he had saved, and the whole family came out to bow in thanks and pressed him to stay and be entertained with food and wine, with the greatest reverence of manner. When the official was warm with wine, he began to talk big, saying: ‘If I had not put forth my strength to save you in those days, you would long ago have died! How could you today have a wife and children, maidservants and servants, a house and property? Today you have money while I, on the contrary, have grown poor. What principle is this?’ Having said his fill, he slept that night in the man’s house. This man then schemed to himself, saying: ‘His hope that I repay him is too excessive! Even if I repay him, I cannot satisfy his mind; and if I do not repay him, then disaster will soon be upon me! Better to take advantage of his sleeping and kill him.’ And so he strangled him with a rope.”

Alas! To save a man and in the end be killed by the very man one saved: here there is indeed a very deep and profound karmic cause. But what dreadful retribution the man who was saved will meet in the future, and the principle by which this official was fated to die a violent death, we shall set aside here and not discuss. The purpose of raising this example is to warn those who bestow kindness yet seek repayment!
Only one who can practice all the many good deeds spoken of above may be called a good person.

From this point, ‘what is called a good person,’ down to ‘immortality may be hoped for,’ the text sets forth how abundant are the blessings of a good person and how they never fail to come true. Know that a good person worthy of the name is one who from the first can distinguish right from wrong without error, and who is complete in both wisdom and courage; and at the last he reaches the state in which ‘self and others are both forgotten,’ dealing with the world and with others in both compassion and forbearance. Moreover, in the intentions he sets up in his mind, in his treatment of himself and of others, he does not in the slightest depart from Heavenly nature and human feeling; even if Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius were born again, they would be of the same mind in this. And what is called a good person is one who follows the Heavenly mind in loving good and keeping far from evil. But how can the human mind be brought to have good and no evil? Because people constantly overlook their own habits and faults, and so lose the original Heavenly mind. Therefore a person should, when good is present, press forward, and when evil is present, reform and repent; only thus may he perhaps attain the state of having good and no evil!

Li Wen Zheng Gong of the Song dynasty, whose given name was Fang, retired in his old age. Because a lantern festival was being held in the palace at the Lantern Festival, Emperor Taizong of Song sent a sedan chair to welcome him into the palace and had him seated beside the emperor. Taizong himself poured wine for him, selected fine fruits with his own hands to bestow on him, and said to him: “You are truly a good man and a gentleman! Twice you have held the office of prime minister, and never once have you had a mind to harm others or injure living things. This is the reason I think of you!” After Wen Zheng Gong returned home, he instructed and encouraged his son, saying: “In this life of mine I have established no wondrous achievement or great merit that could astonish the world; yet I have never covered over the good deeds and good works of others, nor blocked others’ advancement, and even where no other person could see, I have never deceived myself. In dealing with the world, I have kept careful hold of the standard of morality and of my own proper station. These four things I may claim with some confidence not to have violated. Today I have received His Majesty’s praise before a great many ministers as a good man and a gentleman. Know that as for what is called a good man and a gentleman, even Confucius said he had never yet seen one! What sort of person am I, that I should dare to accept the title of good man and gentleman? You should remember His Majesty’s words of excessive praise and reward, and strive to practice the four things I have just spoken of. In this way, toward your ruler you will be loyal, and toward your parents you will be filial; and by this you may cultivate yourself and order your household, and deal with the world and with others, and perhaps thus avoid bringing shame upon the source from which you were born!” His son Zong’e kept careful hold of these instructions, and became a man of considerable repute in the world of his day.

Know that what is called a good person is, to put it simply, one who stops evil and practices good. And if we speak of the utmost reach of this, then to realize the fruit of sagehood, or to cultivate to become an immortal, is likewise nothing but the expansion of this one good thought!

Zou Ziyin of Jiangxi in the Ming dynasty was a Buddhist who deeply revered and had faith in the Three Treasures, and he diligently undertook good works of every kind. Whenever it was a matter of relieving others in distress, or of bringing another’s good work to completion, then though the cold should freeze him or the sun scorch him, he would brave fire and water without declining; and so everyone called him a great good man. After Zou Ziyin fell ill and died, he came before King Yama, and in his heart he was most indignant and unconvinced. King Yama then ordered the recording clerk to open the ledgers of his good and evil and show them to him; and as soon as the ledgers were opened, there were two great characters: ‘fame’ and ‘profit.’ Every good deed Zou Ziyin had done in his whole life was recorded either under the character ‘fame’ or under the character ‘profit’; and only then did Zou Ziyin feel ashamed and accept it. Having come back to life after death, he told others: “Please help me
every

where proclaim to all who do good deeds in the world that they must do good deeds with a sincere heart and in true earnest; and that they must sweep their own minds perfectly clean, and by no means carry a mind of fame and profit into doing good, as I did!” Having said this, five days later Zou Ziyin died. His good friend Tang Shi said: “I knew Ziyin very well. As a man he perhaps could not escape a love of fame; but as for profit, Ziyin was one who made light of wealth and upheld righteousness, so how did he come in the end to love profit? It must be that he acted as intermediary in asking others to help in doing good; his first thought was a vow made for the sake of doing good, but once the money came into his hands, he fell into the fault of occasionally misappropriating the funds for good works. At first he said, ‘I am only borrowing it for the time being’; but as the days grew long, it turned into borrowing under false pretenses and never repaying! This is how Zou Ziyin, in a lifetime of toil and bitter effort at doing good, won no more than the two characters ‘fame’ and ‘profit.’ From this we can see that the underworld often brings to light the hidden and twisted crimes of men; the principle lies exactly here. I was able to comprehend Ziyin’s meaning, and so I have explained it on his behalf. Therefore
every

where proclaim to all who do good deeds in the world that in doing good one should act without acting and yet leave nothing undone, benefiting living beings according to circumstance; this is the highest kind of good. To rescue suffering beings without any thought of repayment, and to urge others to practice good widely, is the second kind of good. To accumulate hidden virtue broadly and seek that after death one not fall into the three evil paths of suffering, this is the third kind of good. If in doing good there is the slightest thought of fame, one has taken the wrong road! And if there is further the slightest greedy thought, putting the funds for good works into one’s own pocket, then in the future one will fall into hell as swiftly as an arrow. Can one not be afraid?” This story is recorded here especially in the hope that those who are willing to do good in the future may understand the principle within it, and earnestly put it into practice!

The good deeds a good person does in his lifetime accord below with the hearts of men, and so all people of the world revere him; they accord above with Heavenly principle, and so the deities of the Heavenly Way protect him. They cause blessings of wealth, honor, long life, health, and peace, and the emoluments of office and rank, all to follow after him, so that he obtains them without seeking; they cause the many evil spirits and fierce ghosts to keep far from him and avoid him, not daring to encroach upon him; and the wise and upright spirits secretly guard and aid him.

All men revere him.’ Goodness is a Heavenly nature inherent in man’s original nature; no sooner is it touched than there is a response. Even among the foolish men and common women, if they hear of a good deed, all will surely praise and commend it; and however fiercely wicked a man may be, when he meets a good person he too dares not encroach upon him. This is because conscience stirs, and naturally there arises a power of self-restraint that keeps him from doing certain things. Why does the text say here that all men revere a good person? It must be that this good person’s virtue truly has in it what deserves reverence, so that there is no one who does not revere him!

When Sima Guang went from Luoyang to the capital to have audience with the emperor, the common people saw Sima Guang on the road and laid their hands upon their foreheads, bowing to him to show their reverence. Wherever Sima Guang went, the common people followed; and the longer they followed, the more numerous they became, until at last the people stopped Sima Guang and said to him: “Your Excellency Sima! We beg you not to go back to Luoyang, but to remain in the capital and help His Majesty govern the realm, so that we common people may have good days!” When Mr. Liu Dajian held office at court, there was no one in the realm who did not sing the praises of his loyalty to the court! When Fu Wenzhong Gong (Fu Bi) rode his donkey to the Tianjin Bridge, the townspeople came running at the news to see him, and the whole city was emptied! When Mr. Shao Kangjie went out to travel, scholars and common people alike, on seeing him, all hurried forward to welcome him; and in their haste some even put their shoes on the wrong feet!

When people rejoice in and admire a good person to such a degree, then the response of Heaven’s will may likewise be known; for if a good person did not truly have in him what deserves reverence, how could he move people to such a degree? And the several good persons spoken of above, while they lived, were either prime ministers or teachers of men; and after death they all became deities.

The Heavenly Way protects him.’ The Heavenly Way is without partiality and without selfishness, yet it constantly responds and communes with good people; and a good person need not say anything, for Heaven will respond to him most subtly. Nor need a good person summon the heavenly deities, for they will come of themselves to protect him! So long as I truly have a good heart and do good deeds, I can move the heavenly deities; and wherever I may be, I will surely receive their protection! Therefore, if one can only strive to do one’s human part with a sincere heart that never slackens, such perseverance to the very end will in the end move Heaven. The Scripture of Deliverance from Calamity says: ‘With the mind thus single, one commits oneself to the will of Heaven’; from this we can see that when a good person does good, there can be no thought of welcoming favor or seeking anything whatsoever! Zhu Xi of the Song dynasty also said: ‘Heaven and Earth do nothing at all; they take the bearing and nourishing of all things as the mind of Heaven and Earth. If a person can keep every thought on benefiting others and aiding things, he is Heaven and Earth himself! For all such a person does accords with the Heavenly mind; how could Heaven not protect him?’

Liu Anshi of the Song dynasty submitted a memorial to the emperor, distinguishing the upright from the wicked among the court ministers, and he spoke in particular of Zhang Dun as a petty man and begged the emperor on no account to employ him, lest he ruin the state and bring harm upon the common people. Later the emperor did not follow Liu Anshi’s advice, but appointed Zhang Dun prime minister; and Liu Anshi was at once stripped of office and banished to a very distant place, crossing mountains and passing over the sea, moved and exiled from place to place with no fixed abode. Everyone said: “Liu Anshi is so advanced in years, and this time, with Zhang Dun taking his revenge and driving him into exile thousands of li away, he is certain to die!” Yet Liu Anshi came through it wholly unharmed, and though he had already reached the age of eighty, he never had a single day’s illness! When Liu Anshi was banished, there was a certain man who, wishing to curry favor with Zhang Dun, sought his instructions and offered to kill Liu Anshi on Zhang Dun’s behalf. But when this man reached the place where Liu Anshi lived and was just about to strike, he was suddenly struck, as it were, by some object, and there on the spot he vomited blood and died.

Tang Ziyu carried his father’s coffin from Sichuan and took ship to return to his old home in Jishui of Jiangxi. It was the season of autumn floods, when the waters of the Qutang River ran all the more swift and fierce,

and it happened too that heavy rain fell from the sky, so that even the boatmen were filled with dread. Ziyu was overcome with grief, fearing that he could not carry his father’s coffin home, and he wept aloud toward Heaven; and no sooner had he cried out once than the river withdrew more than twenty fathoms at the sound. Only after the boat he was on had passed did the river return and flow back again, as turbulent as before. Know that loyalty and filial piety are the first of moral duties, and therefore the deities of the Heavenly Way thus protect those who are wholly loyal and wholly filial!

Blessing and emolument follow after him.’ In sages, worthies, and gentlemen, their words are good and their deeds are good, and the harmonious breath of their hearts moves Heaven; and so auspicious omens and blessings naturally follow after them. The Book of Songs says: ‘Rejoice, O gentleman, blessing and emolument are renewed upon you.’ This is just the saying that blessing and emolument follow after him!

Guo Ziyi, the great general of the Tang dynasty, recovered the two capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang during the An Lushan rebellion, and his merit overshadowed the world, surpassing that of all the meritorious ministers of the Tang house; for upon him hung the safety of the common people of the realm for as long as thirty years! The emperor enfeoffed him as Prince of Fenyang, and his personal wealth, honor, and long life may be said to have reached the utmost extreme; moreover, of his sons and grandsons, nearly every one was prosperous, distinguished, and noble. This is truly rare in all ages past and present, and beyond the reach of others to compare with!

Know that the reason Guo Ziyi could possess such great blessing and such abundant emolument was that he had established great merit for the realm and the state, and that his own virtue had likewise reached a considerable height; and only so could he enjoy such blessing and abundant emolument. This is by no means something that could be obtained by mere chance!

In Fengyang of Anhui in the Ming dynasty there was a man named Zheng Zhao. One night he dreamed that he had come to the Heavenly court, and saw that the heavenly deities had already prepared a seat for him and were waiting for him. And they said to him: “By your original lot you belonged to the poor and humble; but because you have done good with all your might, I have commanded the two deities of blessing and emolument to follow after you, and hereafter you shall sit in this seat prepared for you in advance.” Zheng Zhao was awakened by this, and his good thoughts grew all the firmer, and his fame all the more resounding. Wherever he went, wealth came with him; wherever he arrived, blessing and emolument descended with him. His sons and grandsons were many, and all were wealthy and noble and enjoyed great blessing. In the end he cultivated the Way and, after his deliverance from the corpse, truly realized the rank of the Perfected Man of Pure Desire.

At this point someone may raise a doubt: Yan Yuan was a sage, so why did he die young, and in a mean alley besides? Yi and Qi were also sages and worthies, so why did they starve to death on Mount Shouyang? Why was Yuan Xian poor, and why was Fan Pang condemned and beheaded? Know that the moral cultivation of these several sages and worthies had all reached a very high realm; it was only that their destinies lacked blessing and emolument. Yet the good virtue in which they stood can contend for brightness with the sun and moon, and is not to be compared with ordinary blessing and emolument. This too is a principle that those who would die for benevolence and take righteousness should understand!

The many evil spirits keep far from him.’ Evil and upright cannot stand together; where the upright is, the evil naturally cannot abide. It is like the sun coming out, whereupon ice and snow of themselves melt away. Li Jifu said: ‘The deities love uprightness; if a person can hold fast to uprightness, he will receive the protection of the deities. And demons and ghosts cannot overcome a man of virtue; but if he loses his virtue, then demons and ghosts will flourish!’ This too is a natural principle.

In the Ming dynasty there was a scholar named Jing Qing. When he was on his way to the metropolitan examination and passed through Chunhua County, he lodged for the night with a local family. Now the daughter of that household was possessed by a demon. On the night Jing Qing lodged there, strange to say, the demon did not come at all; but after Jing Qing had left, the demon came again. The girl then asked the demon: ‘Why did you not come last night?’ The demon said: ‘It was because I was keeping out of the way of Scholar Jing that I did not come!’ The daughter told her father of this, and her father at once set off in pursuit of Jing Qing. Jing Qing then wrote the four characters ‘Jing Qing is here’ and told her father to paste them on the door; and from that time on the demon no longer dared to come. Jing Qing was a man of the utmost uprightness and loyal fierceness, and to this day he is still held in admiration.

Know that what can fill and pervade the space between Heaven and Earth is upright qi! If a person’s qi can be without cowardice and without a guilty heart, then it can flow grandly and freely, and demons and ghosts, seeing it, will of themselves withdraw. Therefore a gentleman has the discipline of nourishing his qi, and the key to nourishing qi lies in governing the mind. If one can attain clarity and brightness abiding in oneself, and dwell in sincerity and calm stability, then the so-called demons and ghosts will have nowhere to hide. But if a person’s mind has anything murky or furtive in it, then he need not ask whether demons and ghosts have come, for his own mind has already become a place filled with demons and ghosts; how then could he, like Jing Qing, cause demons and ghosts, the moment they see him, to be subdued by his upright qi? Deities and men are of one principle: a good person whom men revere will be protected by the deities as well. It is as they say, that when virtue is weighty, even ghosts and spirits will admire him!

Han Qi of the Song dynasty was complete in both civil and martial talents; he went out as a general and came in as a minister. When he was serving as a military commander garrisoned in a distant region, it happened that his army was moved from Chengde to Zhongshan, and as it was crossing the Sha River, the advance party he had sent out suddenly reported back to him: ‘General, the waters of the river upstream have suddenly broken forth, and the flood is nearly upon us!’ Han Qi at once issued an urgent order for the officers and men to prepare boats to cross the river; and sure enough the river came on in surging waves, toppling mountains and overturning seas, so that the boats were nearly capsized, and the officers and men were filled with alarm and terror. At that very moment a divine dragon suddenly halted in the upper reaches of the river and blocked the onrushing flood, and the river at once grew calm. Only after Han Qi’s army had crossed in safety did the divine dragon depart, whereupon the river again rose in flood, as fierce as before.

In Yizheng of the Ming dynasty there was an old man surnamed Jin whose family ran a pawnshop. In the early years of the Jiajing reign, river pirates plundered and pillaged everywhere, and nearly every wealthy household in the region was robbed; only the Jin family was not robbed, and so the authorities suspected the Jin family of colluding with the bandits. Later the bandits were caught by the authorities, who questioned them: ‘Why did you rob every family but the Jin family?’ The bandits said: ‘Every time we went to rob the Jin family, we were driven off by the golden-armored deity!’ The authorities did not believe the bandits’ story, so they summoned the local constable and the neighbors to question them, and they all said: ‘The Jin family was not robbed, and truly it is because the Jin family has accumulated virtue! Every pawnshop buys in at a low price when the pledge is made, and demands a high price when it is redeemed; only the Jin family’s pawnshop is fair in both directions, sets a high valuation, and allows a long term. Moreover, when the aged and the poor pawn their goods, the Jin family makes an exception and waives the interest. In winter they waive the interest on pawned winter clothing, and in summer they waive the interest on pawned summer clothing; the Jin family has done this every year! Heaven protects the good, and so commanded the golden-armored deity to guard and protect the Jin family; there is nothing doubtful in this principle!’ When the county magistrate heard this, he too commended Old Man Jin’s good conduct, and moreover submitted a memorial to the court, and the court issued an order praising and honoring the good deeds of the Jin family.

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: ‘In the foregoing, when calamity and evil were spoken of, it was first said that all men hate him; now, when blessing and good are spoken of, it is first said that all men revere him. For the calamities sent down by baleful stars and fierce spirits, and such matters as the protection and guarding of the deities, may for a time perhaps not be seen; but that all men revere and all men hate are trustworthy early signs and omens! One who has the mind to learn the Way should constantly turn this over in reflection. If the number of those who revere me grows ever greater, then I may know the degree to which the deities protect and guard me; and if the number of those who hate me grows ever greater, then I may know that baleful stars and fierce spirits are glaring down upon my head in wrath! This is the principle that the hearts of men are the will of Heaven; there is no need to insist on inquiring into what we can neither see nor hear!’
They cause the undertakings of a good person surely to succeed and to be immortal, and one may further hope to become an immortal and have one’s name enrolled in the Heavenly court!

There is no undertaking in the world that cannot be brought to success, and all people under Heaven are capable of undertaking it! Only do good with a true and sincere heart; then since human affairs accord with the Heavenly mind, how could the will of Heaven run counter to human wishes? It will of itself secretly aid the good person, and there is no good work that cannot be carried through and accomplished!

Tai Shang was the founding patriarch of the Daoists, and so he concerned himself especially with the principles of seeking immortality. Mencius said: ‘Every man can become a Yao or a Shun.’ Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan school in China, said: ‘Simply use this mind, and straightway accomplish Buddhahood.’ Why is it that what the sages of the three teachings say is almost exactly the same? Immortality may be hoped for, Buddhahood may be cultivated and attained, and Yao and Shun may be equaled! How much more, then, may worldly fame and rank, wealth and honor, long life, and sons and daughters be sought and obtained? All this depends only on whether the one who seeks earnestly puts it into practice!

The Buddha says in the Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching: ‘You monks should be diligent and press forward, and then there is nothing too difficult! It is like a thin stream of water flowing without cease: in the course of a very long time it can bore through hard stone. But if the mind of the practitioner is often slack and halts, it is like drilling wood to make fire, and stopping to rest before the wood is even warm; though one may wish to obtain fire, that is impossible!’

Master Lianchi of the Ming dynasty said: ‘In any single skill or art in the world, at the beginning of learning it seems exceedingly difficult, as though it were utterly impossible to master; and so one sets it aside and does not learn it, and in that way one never masters it at all. Therefore, at the very first, what is precious is a firm and undoubting mind. Yet even though one has resolve and no doubt, if one is leisurely and slow and does not learn earnestly, one still cannot succeed! Next, what is precious is a mind of vigor and courage. Yet even though one is vigorous, one may be satisfied by some small attainment, or grow weary because the time is long, or be deluded and turned about by favorable circumstances, or fall away when meeting adverse ones; and then one still cannot succeed! Next again, what is precious is a mind that is constant and enduring and never retreats; only this is to be called a true man of resolve! If a person can keep his mind thus, what is there that he cannot accomplish? You should all encourage yourselves!’

Li Duanyuan, Grand Commandant of the Song dynasty, asked Chan Master Daguan: ‘As for heaven and hell, do they exist or do they not?’ The master replied: ‘The Buddhas speak of existence where there is no existence, like a diseased eye that sees flowers in the sky; Your Excellency seeks non-existence within existence, like using your hand to scoop up the moon in the water. This is as laughable as seeing a prison before your eyes yet not knowing to avoid it, or hearing of heaven outside the mind yet wishing to be born there! You do not know that delight and terror are both within our single mind, and that heaven and hell are both states created by the good and evil of the mind. Your Excellency, only understand your own mind, and naturally there will be no delusion or affliction.’

According to the records of the immortals in the Daoist scriptures, they number as many as ninety-nine thousand and nine hundred and ninety thousand, and all of them succeeded in their cultivation by piling up merit and accumulating virtue while in the world! For example, Mr. He Xizhi, because he wrote a commentary on the Diamond Sutra and thereby helped purify the hearts of the world, after his death held the office of Inspector of the Calendar and Chronology of the Western Marchmount; and though he was in the Marchmount’s bureau, he too was one who received deliverance. This is the principle that by doing good one may hope to become an immortal. From ancient times to the present, those who became immortals number more than a hundred thousand; and so it is said: ‘Say not that there is nowhere to learn to be an immortal; through the ages, how many have ascended!’ People today cultivate the Way but lack a true heart, and when they fail to succeed themselves, they say: ‘There are no immortals in the world.’ This is just like studying Confucius and Mencius yet being unable to put the words and deeds of Confucius and Mencius into practice, and then saying that there are no sages and worthies in the world. Both are wrong.

One who wishes to seek to become a heavenly immortal should accumulate one thousand three hundred good deeds; doing one good deed a day, in only four years he can succeed. One who wishes to seek to become an earthly immortal should accumulate three hundred good deeds; doing one good deed a day, in only one year he can succeed.

This section sums up the foregoing and sets forth the doing of good as the fundamental method of becoming an immortal. The one thousand and the three hundred spoken of here fix the number and the term of the good deeds; if one only does them earnestly, success is certain, and there is also the sense that one will not retreat. And the difference between heavenly immortals and earthly immortals lies in how many good deeds they have done. The Shurangama Sutra says: ‘There are ten kinds of immortals. The first is called the earth-walking immortal, the second the flying immortal, the third the roaming immortal, the fourth the sky-walking immortal, the fifth the heaven-walking immortal, the sixth the all-penetrating immortal, the seventh the Way-walking immortal, the eighth the illumining immortal, the ninth the refined immortal, and the tenth the absolute immortal. Though their lifespans may reach a thousand or ten thousand years, they are still within the six paths of rebirth!’ Therefore, after succeeding in becoming an immortal, one must still go one step further from the top of a hundred-foot pole; only thus will one not fall back again, but rise higher still, and leap out of the three realms and the six paths of rebirth. It was thus with the immortal Lü Dongbin, who heard the principle set forth in the Diamond Sutra, ‘one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere,’ and was thereby suddenly enlightened; afterwards he met Chan Master Huanglong, who alone confirmed his awakening for him. And the Perfected Man Sun Simiao often sought instruction in the Buddhadharma from the Tang dynasty Vinaya Master Daoxuan, and later went to Chengdu in Sichuan and heard the nameless wandering monk expound the Jeweled Stupa Chapter of the sutra, whereby he was able to realize the rank of Perfected Man. These are good examples of going one step further from the top of a hundred-foot pole.

Zhongli of the Han dynasty transmitted his method of refining the elixir to Lü Dongbin: by dotting it upon iron, the iron could be turned to gold, which could then be used to relieve the poor of the world. Lü Dongbin asked Zhongli: ‘Once it has turned to gold, will it in the end turn back to iron again?’ Zhongli answered: ‘After five hundred years it will still turn back to its original iron.’ Lü Dongbin said: ‘If so, then it will harm the people of five hundred years hence. I am unwilling to do such a thing.’ Zhongli had taught Lü Dongbin to turn iron into gold only to test his heart. Now that he knew Lü Dongbin’s heart was good, he said to him: ‘To cultivate immortality one must accumulate three thousand meritorious deeds; hearing these words of yours, your three thousand meritorious deeds are already complete.’
If anyone acts contrary to righteousness and gives rise to evil thoughts, or goes against Heavenly principle and does evil deeds.

From this section down to ‘and death likewise overtakes him,’ Tai Shang sets out in detail the doing of evil and the inviting of calamity. These two sentences are the general outline of doing evil, and also the starting point of those who do evil; they stand in exact opposition to the two sentences spoken earlier, ‘if it accords with the Way, then advance.’

The ancients said: ‘Man’s nature is like water, and the rules of propriety and law must serve as its dikes. If the dikes are not built firmly enough, in the end they will surely burst, and the water will rush and race in every direction, overflow, and become a disaster. If man’s nature is not restrained and controlled, then he will surely become unbridled, break the law and violate discipline, and the world will fall into great disorder! Therefore, to remove affliction and desire, to still the deluded mind, to forbid the doing of evil, and to stop perverse conduct, one must not forget the rules of propriety and law for even a single moment!’ It is also said: ‘That a fine horse galloping forward dares not run wild at will is chiefly because there is a
rein

to control it! Though a petty man be rude and unreasonable, yet he dares not indulge himself beyond measure and without restraint, because there is the punishment of the law and its penalties to restrain him. And our own consciousness dares not casually give rise to thoughts and go climbing after conditions everywhere, because the mind has the work of mindful awareness. Therefore, if a person within has no power of mindful awareness, it is like a fine horse with no
rein
to control it, or a petty man with no threat of the law to deter him: how then could one cut off the greed and desire within the mind, or counter the deluded thoughts in the heart?’

Suo Jingxu was a man of great love of learning and eager to advance. The prefectural and commandery officials of the place where he lived deeply admired his learning and character, and frequently sent letters inviting Suo Jingxu to banquets at the government offices; but Suo Jingxu never accepted. The governor at that time was named Yin Dan. He once paid a visit in person to Suo Jingxu’s home and talked with him so delightfully that he quite forgot the time to go home. After conversing with Suo Jingxu, Governor Yin Dan sighed and said: ‘What the ordinary worldly view regards as wealth and honor is not the wealth and honor inherent in one’s nature! And so the eye loves to strain outward after fine colors, and the ear loves to drown itself in sounds; but Mr. Suo is exactly the opposite of the worldly view. Worldly people love to chase after the enjoyments of the senses and lose themselves in the excitements of sound and light; but Mr. Suo’s body, though it dwells here in this dusty world, has a mind that perches and rests upon righteousness and Heavenly principle! How could external conditions and circumstances ever move his heart? Know that Mr. Suo’s understanding of righteousness and Heavenly principle is most deep and clear; therefore in dealing with the world he naturally holds fast to righteousness and follows Heavenly principle.’

The reason people today dare to act contrary to righteousness and give rise to evil thoughts, or to go against Heavenly principle and do wicked things, is simply that their understanding and realization of righteousness and Heavenly principle is not clear enough! Why not go and learn from Mr. Suo Jingxu?
On the contrary, they take doing evil to be capability.

The phrase ‘taking evil as capability’ is spoken specifically with regard to human affairs. Human nature is originally good, yet some people take doing evil to be capability; this is to lose the very substance of their good nature. Moreover, these four words ‘taking evil as capability’ are the fundamental reason why evildoers great and small throughout the ages have done evil, and that is why it is placed at the head of all evils. However stupid a person may be, there is none who is willing to be an evildoer; yet neither is there any who does not wish to be a capable person. It is only that they mistake this word ‘capable,’ and so they go on doing worse and worse. At first they say: ‘The capable man is useful, and the incapable man is useless; the capable man is feared and dreaded by others, so that they dare not bully him, while the incapable man is bullied everywhere.’ Then, after a long time, they themselves know the wicked things they have done; and so they brazenly take their stand as evildoers, and no longer conceal it, and even give it fair names! For example, the greedy man uses power, cunning, and deceit to seize the wealth of others, and takes this as his capability; and he even gives it the fair name of ‘strategy.’ The ruthless man uses force, trickery, and underhanded means to ensnare others, and takes this as his capability; and he even gives it the fair name of a ‘ruthless hand.’ The lecherous man uses deceit, cunning, and coquetry to entice the wives and daughters of others, and takes this as his capability; and he even gives it the fair name of ‘romance.’ The flatterer takes fawning, toadying, and cheating as his capability; and he even gives it the fair name of ‘cleverness.’ The slanderer takes spreading rumors and stirring up trouble as his capability, and actually gives it the fair name of ‘eloquence.’ There is no end to the list of such things; everyone vies in splendor and competes in oddity, each striving to outdo the other, seeing who is the more brilliant and who the more formidable. Hypocritical people feel no doubt about such doings, and ordinary hearers take such words for wise sayings! And so, whenever they happen upon someone with no strategy, no ruthless hand, no romance, no cleverness, and no eloquence, there is no one who does not laugh at him as a discarded timber of this world and a waste of his age! But when the evil deeds are all done and retribution has arrived, and the lid is laid upon the coffin and the verdict given, then those so-called capable people are truly too many to count! And where are they all now? Therefore I exhort all people of the world: better by far to bend for a while and be what others call discarded timber and waste, while you yourself firmly work away at the depths of your own mind. This is plain indeed, yet it has flavor, and it is exceedingly stable, and it will never fail! If you do not believe this truth, then I beg you to observe the good people of this world: there is not one who does not obtain the protection of Heaven and the reverence of all men; and of evil people, there is not one who does not receive the condemnation of Heaven and the loathing of men!

The Buddha said: ‘All evildoers in the world fall into hell after death. In hell there is a master named Ox-Head Asura, exceedingly fierce and venomous, with not a shred of compassion or forbearance. When he sees the beings who have fallen into hell undergoing all manner of painful retribution, his only concern is that they are not yet in enough pain and not yet dealt with viciously enough. Someone asked the jailer: “The pain suffered by the beings in hell is boundless and measureless, and truly it moves one to grief and pity; why is it that you constantly harbor cruelty and venom, and have no heart of kindness and compassion?” The jailer replied: “These beings who suffer in hell are all those who were unfilial to their parents, slandered the Three Treasures, reviled their relatives, slighted their teachers and elders, framed good people, and killed living beings, and who created many evil deeds! Moreover, when these offenders come to hell to suffer, and whenever the time comes for them to leave hell and be reborn, we exhort them with all our might, saying: The extreme suffering in hell is most hard to endure! Now that your karmic suffering is finished and you may leave hell, we hope that after you go out you will on no account do evil again! But these offenders will often refuse to repent; today they leave hell, and before long they have come back again! Thus they pass through birth and death over and over, and do not know suffering! For this reason I have not the least compassion for offenders!” From this we know that those who do evil will surely fall into hell. Now that we have obtained this brief span of time and dwell in this world, we ought to practice kindness with all our strength, cultivate all good widely, dissolve the three obstructions and afflictions, purify the six sense faculties, recite the Buddha’s name and observe the fasts, practice Chan and learn the Way, and leap out of the bitter sea of birth and death within the six paths of rebirth. On no account give free rein to the afflictions of the three poisons, greed, hatred, and delusion, and do the evil deeds of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct! Know that whoever creates evil deeds will surely receive evil retribution, and that all the Buddha said is true and not false; we should earnestly believe and uphold it!’

Yu Sixuan of the Tang dynasty was exceedingly clever and ingenious. Empress Wu Zetian wished to build a kind of report box, to be used especially for people to denounce and expose the private secrets of others. Of all the craftsmen, not one could make such a box; but Yu Sixuan was able to make it, and it moreover matched Empress Wu’s conception exactly. Later someone dropped a secret letter into the box, exposing that Yu Sixuan had once, in Yangzhou, made for Xu Jingye a kind of blade-wheel weapon, used on the battlefield especially to charge the ranks of the army and to kill and wound many of the court’s officers and men. Yu Sixuan was condemned to death on this account.

In the time of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty, Song Sheng in the early years of the Zhenghe reign held the office of transport commissioner of Jingxi and was in charge of the works of building the Western Inner Palace. He once said to others: ‘If this project is finished quickly, we shall at once receive the emperor’s reward.’ Among the materials for the project, ox bone was often needed for mixing with the lime; later the ox bone ran short, and so Song Sheng ordered men to dig up the bones of the unclaimed dead and burn them to bone ash, to replace the ox bone ash. At the time his deputy, the transport judge Sun Kuang, tried to dissuade him, but Song Sheng would not listen to Sun Kuang’s remonstrance, and Sun Kuang had no choice but to plead illness, resign his office, and leave. Later, because he had completed the work in good time, Song Sheng was promoted by the emperor to Grand Secretary. It was then that he suddenly contracted a strange illness, and moreover spoke to himself, saying: ‘My sin in digging up graves and stealing and burning human bones ought to bring the extinction of my whole house!’ Having said this, he vomited blood and died; and before long every member of Song Sheng’s household had also died. Later, when Sun Kuang fell ill and died, he came to the underworld and saw Song Sheng lying upon red-hot iron beds and copper pillars, undergoing punishment, his whole body covered in blood. Sun Kuang then walked on to another great hall, where he saw the underworld official, who said to him: ‘Sun Kuang, you once tried to dissuade Song Sheng from burning human bones; when Song Sheng would not listen, you resigned your office and went home. You are truly a man of conscience! Your lifespan shall be extended by twelve years.’ Sun Kuang thereupon returned to life and came back to the world of the living, and told others of this matter. Know that the most grievous calamity under Heaven is none other than the extinction of one’s house and clan! Song Sheng, because he gave rise to a thought of coveting reward, thereupon committed the great evil of burning human bones, and before long met the calamity of the extinction of his house. The ancients once said: ‘Evil arises because of greed, and so greed is the root of evil; therefore the most important method of curing evil is to remove greed.’ These are true words!

The Scripture of Central Admonition says: ‘If a person does one evil deed, his mind and spirit will be unsettled; if he does ten evil deeds, his qi will be depleted and his body weak; if he does twenty evil deeds, his fate will be full of setbacks, his wealth will be broken and decline, and nothing will go as he wishes; if he does fifty evil deeds, he will end his life with no spouse; if he does a hundred evil deeds, he will meet with flood or fire, or be dragged down by sudden calamity and condemned to a death that is no death at all; if he does five hundred evil deeds, his line will be cut off and he will have neither sons nor grandsons; and if he does a thousand evil deeds, a treasonous minister or rebellious son will appear in his house, who will commit crimes that reach the heavens, so that the whole household is wiped out and the descendants of every generation will have their bodily forms changed and fall among the birds and beasts. Know that when evil has been piled up to the full and overflowing, the calamity will reach even the sons and grandsons of later generations, and that one’s own fall into hell is still the lighter punishment! Every person should keep this lesson constantly in mind, and then he will naturally not do evil!’
To harden the heart and do what injures and harms living creatures.

This sentence is spoken specifically with regard to living creatures. Heaven has the virtue of loving life, yet some people harbor cruelty in their hearts and do the work of maiming and killing living creatures. Know that maiming living creatures is the gravest of evil deeds; and if the motive moreover springs from cruelty, then such a person will do whatever his will inclines to, without a shred of compassion or pity! The root of all good lies in a compassionate heart, and the root of all evil lies in cruelty; therefore to remove cruelty and preserve compassion is precisely where the cultivation of sages and worthies, of the immortals, and of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas lies!

To fear death and cling to life, to love one’s own kin and old friends, to know what pain is and to feel what suffering is: in these clingings and feelings, animals and human beings are exactly alike! But human beings have intelligence while animals lack it; human beings can speak while animals cannot; human beings are strong while animals are weak. Now consider the people who set out a single table of food: they do not kill only one living creature. For example, to make a single meat soup of turtledoves, pigeons, quail, and sparrows, more than ten lives must be killed; and to make one dish or one soup of mussels, clams, shrimps, and cockles, more than a hundred lives must be killed! And there are those who love fine food and exhaust every device: eating them raw and roasting them alive, cutting open their bellies and splitting their breasts, stripping off their skins and prying open their shells, carrying cruelty to its utmost extreme. After a single full meal they are smug and pleased with themselves; but if there is the slightest delay or inattention, they lose their temper and curse the cook. So if one only thinks it over calmly, it is truly a thing to make one tremble with horror and mourn!

The sutra says: ‘There is no living creature that does not dread the pain of the knife and the club, and none that does not cherish its own life!’ And so, when Wang Ke was about to kill a sheep, the sheep ran toward Wang Ke’s guest and knelt down to him, pleading for its life; when Zou Sheng was about to kill a deer, the deer knelt down and wept. Again, when Shen Neihan was serving as assistant prefect in Jiangning, the cook was about to kill a sheep, but the knife kept disappearing; afterwards it was discovered that the sheep had carried the knife off in its mouth and hidden it beneath the wall! And when Yang Jie was serving as judicial commissioner, he once went sightseeing at Mount Ayuwang; as he slept by day he dreamed that more than a hundred women came before him, seeming to plead with him about something. When he woke he went quietly to the kitchen to look, and understood that it was the clams sending him a dream to plead for their lives! From this we may know that animals too cherish their own lives in this way, and are no different from human beings. And if a person is accidentally scalded by hot water or fire, or cut by a knife or needle, he will surely cry out to Heaven and knock his head on the ground, calling for help; and at the slightest dizziness of the head or pain of the eye, he will clamor to see a physician or buy medicine. If a person so cherishes his own body, why does he feel no pity or tender care for the lives of animals, but maims and kills them at will, grudging not to form enmity with them and create the karma of killing? Alas! Of all evil karma, this one is the most grievous! The Buddhas and bodhisattvas and all the heavenly immortals exhort us not to kill living beings. Know that karmic retribution misses nothing by a hair’s breadth; one should put oneself in the other’s place and measure his heart by one’s own, and at once and sharply awaken. Therefore the various reasons why domestic fowl and beasts may not be slaughtered are set out here in detail, and all men of benevolence are entreated to observe and practice them with all their strength!

First, one ought not to kill on one’s birthday. The Book of Songs says: ‘Alas, alas, my parents, how they toiled to give me birth!’ The day on which one’s mother gave one birth is called the day of the mother’s peril. Therefore on one’s birthday one ought above all to abstain from killing and observe the fast, and to do good widely; thus one may add blessing and length of years to one’s parents. And if both parents have already passed away, one may by this merit cause their spirits to obtain rebirth in a higher realm at an earlier day. How then can one forget that this day is the day of one’s mother’s suffering, and give free rein to the cravings of one’s own mouth and belly, killing living beings and eating their flesh? This will drag down one’s parents and bring harm to oneself as well! Yet this practice has long been the custom of most people in the whole world, and they do not even feel that it is wrong; truly it makes those of conscience weep and grieve!

Second, one ought not to kill when a child is born. All people grieve if they have no child of their own, and rejoice when they have one; yet they never reflect that all birds and beasts love their young as well! Now to celebrate the birth of one’s own child, one kills the young of birds and beasts: can the heart be at peace in this? Moreover, when a baby has just been born, one does not accumulate blessing and seek long life for him, but on the contrary creates for him the karma of killing: such conduct is truly most foolish! Yet this practice has long been the custom of most people in the whole world, and they do not even feel that it is wrong; truly it makes those of conscience weep and sigh in grief!

Third, one ought not to kill in funerals or in sacrifices to ancestors. In conducting funerals or in sacrificing to ancestors, or in sweeping the tombs at Qingming, one ought to abstain from killing, in order to increase the otherworldly blessings of the departed kin and ancestors; for if one kills living beings to make the offerings, one only vainly adds to the evil karma of the departed spirits and ancestors. Not only is there no benefit, but there is harm instead; and so a wise person will absolutely never do it. Yet this practice has long been the custom of most people in the whole world, and they do not even feel that it is wrong; truly it makes those of conscience weep and sigh in grief!

Fourth, one ought not to kill at weddings. In the weddings of the world, from the first meeting through the betrothal to the marriage itself, who knows how many living beings are killed! Know that the marriage of husband and wife is the beginning of continuing the family line and bearing and raising children; on this fine day and in this lovely season, a day of good fortune and rejoicing, to do a deed of violence and kill living beings to feast the guests is already to plant the evil cause of future vengeance! That is, it is to gather the machinery of killing and the seeds of hatred within the women’s quarters! Yet this practice has long been the custom of most people in the whole world, and they do not even feel that it is wrong; truly it makes those of conscience grieve and sigh on their behalf!

Fifth, one ought not to kill when seeking blessings. When ordinary people fall ill, they often kill living beings to sacrifice to the deities, hoping to beseech the deities to send down blessing and protection; yet they never reflect that the very purpose of their sacrifice to the gods is to be spared death and to obtain long life! Now to kill another’s life in order to prolong my own life is a great violation of Heavenly principle and of conscience, and truly there is nothing graver than this! Know that ‘the wise and upright are the gods’; how could the gods have selfish partiality? Such seeking of blessing not only cannot prolong one’s life, but vainly adds to one’s own karma of killing!

Sixth, one ought not to kill when making vows. Know the principle that ‘the impartial are the Buddhas, and the upright are the gods’: the Buddhas and bodhisattvas and the deities will absolutely never accept a bribe and send down blessing upon the one who bribes them! When people today make vows before the deities and then slaughter living creatures, the vow so made is called an evil vow! And even if the vow is granted, evil retribution is waiting just behind!

Seventh, one ought not to kill when entertaining guests. On a fine day and in a lovely season, with worthy hosts and excellent guests, when friends gather for a feast, even vegetable dishes and soups of greens would not hinder the affection and the leisurely good cheer between host and guest! Why must one slaughter livestock with all one’s might and eat and drink to excess? Know that while host and guest laugh and feast and eat their fill in the hall, the livestock being chopped, killed, fried, roasted, and boiled in the kitchen are there wailing and weeping; yet host and guest turn a deaf ear, and how could they ever comprehend the suffering of being cooked in the pot!

Eighth, one ought not to kill in making a living. People of the world, for the sake of a livelihood, take up trades that kill living beings, such as hunting and fishing, or the trade of the butcher, to earn money and support their families; yet know that Heaven never gives birth to a person who has no allotted sustenance! So long as one possesses a single skill or a single talent, one can earn money and eat one’s fill; why must one take up this evil trade of killing living beings to support one’s family? This not only violates Heavenly principle, but the more one kills, the poorer one becomes! Therefore of those who take up the trade of killing and yet grow wealthy, not one in a hundred can be found! Moreover it plants the deep cause of unfilial children in this present life and of hell hereafter, and brings evil retribution in lives to come. There is nothing graver than this; why will they not change their trade and seek another livelihood?

Giving gifts is in itself a fine courtesy, but when the gift is live chickens and ducks, fish and shrimps, then one has already stirred and awakened the machinery of killing! As for oneself, one has killed living beings on another’s behalf and must bear that offense alone; and as for the one who receives the gift, he merely eats his fill, so that neither party gains any merit at all. As for keeping goldfish, the tiny shrimps used as their food must be counted in the tens of thousands; and to keep white cranes, the small fish used must number a thousand lives. All these are karma of killing; one must not be heedless!

What has been said above is only a rough sketch in brief; people should extend the principle from it, and then their hearts will naturally come to have the measure of that which covers them like heaven and bears them up like earth.

Mr. Huang Luzhi once composed a verse that says: ‘My flesh and the flesh of living beings: the names differ, the substance does not; originally we share one nature, only our bodily forms are apart. Their pain and affliction are borne by them, while fat and sweet things are what I require. Do not let King Yama pass the sentence; search your own heart and see what you would deserve.’

Lü Dongbin, the immortal of the Tang dynasty, also spoke a verse: ‘If you would prolong your life, hear my words: in all things be alert and clear, and be sure to forgive your own faults. If you would prolong your life, you must set living creatures free; this is the true principle of cause and effect. When another is dying, if you save him, then when you are dying, Heaven will save you. To prolong life and beget children there is no other way: refrain from killing and set living beings free, and that is all!’

Xu Zhenjun was a man of Runan in the Jin dynasty, and from childhood he loved to hunt. One day he went up into the mountains to hunt and shot a young deer; and he saw the mother deer keep licking the young deer’s wound with her tongue, as though her grief were without limit, and before long the mother deer too fell dead. Xu Zhenjun then cut open the mother deer’s breast and belly with his knife, and discovered that her liver and intestines were broken into pieces. He was greatly moved and his remorse was without end; and thereupon he broke his bow and arrows and swore never to hunt again. Xu Zhenjun was afterwards recommended as a filial and incorrupt candidate and served as magistrate of Jingyang County. Because he was troubled by the disorder of the Jin court’s government, he gave up his office and withdrew from the world, and followed Wu Meng in the study of the Way. In the second year of the Taikang reign of Emperor Xiaowu of Jin, he attained the Way and became a Perfected Man on the Western Mountain of Hongzhou. Because he often manifested his numinous power to aid the world, the emperor of Song posthumously enfeoffed him as the Perfected Man of Divine Merit and Wondrous Salvation, commonly called Xu Zhenjun, or else Xu Jingyang.

There was a merchant named Ren Tianyi, a man greedy for profit and cruel of heart. Every year he would go to Qingkou in Haizhou to buy salted pigs and bring them back for slaughter. Once, carrying salted pigs by boat, as he passed the Liuan Canal lock at Gaoyou, a great wind rose in the night; the boat was overturned by the wind, and the pigs were at once snatched up and scattered by the fishermen. Ren Tianyi was on the bank secretly bewailing his loss, when the great mast of the boat happened to fall over upon him, crushing Ren Tianyi into a flat cake of flesh.

Know that if wealth is in one’s destiny, one can earn money wherever one goes! Why then take up a trade that kills living beings and destroys life? Merchants who meet retribution like that of Ren Tianyi are truly too many to count, and they are worth reflecting on deeply, lest for the sake of a livelihood one instead set foot on the road of death. As for being burned and plundered by thieves and robbers, or even drowned in water and the like, it is not unlikely that Heaven was taking his life in return for the offenses of his killing!
Toward loyal, honest, and good people, one should cherish them, recommend them, and praise them; yet instead one secretly schemes to injure them.

Secret injury means injuring another by covert scheme, such as shooting an arrow from the dark, which is hardest of all to guard against; and moreover the other is harmed by me while I do not have to bear the evil name of one who harms others. This is the worst of wicked deeds. Toward ordinary people it is already impermissible to injure another by such covert schemes; how much less permissible is it to injure good and kind people with them! For good people are the hope upon which the common folk rest. When a good person is in a state, he will be valued by the people of that state; when a good person is in a village, he will be valued by all the people of the village. So how can one covertly scheme to injure a good person?

Li Linfu, prime minister of the Tang dynasty, was a man of sinister cunning who injured the good, and the evil deeds he did were too many to enumerate. When Li Linfu was about to fall, he saw a demonic creature with saw-like teeth and hook-like claws, covered all over with hair and with eyes like lightning, which struck him with its hand; and before long Li Linfu died with blood flowing from all seven openings of his head. After Li Linfu died, the court issued an order stripping him of his rank; and moreover his coffin was broken open, his corpse was mutilated, and his sons and grandsons were exiled to the region of Lingnan. In the early years of the Chunxi reign of the Song dynasty, in the district of Hanzhou, a woman was struck dead by lightning, and red characters were written upon her body, saying: ‘Li Linfu was disloyal as a minister, and covertly injured the good. For three lives he shall be a prostitute, and for seven lives an ox; and when these retributions are finished, he shall fall forever among the water-dwelling creatures.’

When a petty man injures a gentleman and by luck succeeds, he says that the gentleman’s life and death are controlled by his own hand. He does not know that even if the gentleman dies by his hand, it is because the gentleman had formerly formed a grievance with him, and only thus did such a result come about; but if the gentleman had never formed a grievance with anyone, then no matter how formidable the petty man might be, in the end he could not kill him. And when an evil man harms another, it is like spitting at the sky: he not only fails to spit upon the sky, but the spittle falls back upon his own face! Therefore one must not slander or injure worthy and good people, for in the end it is oneself that is harmed!
Toward one’s ruler, the head of state, and one’s parents, one should be loyal, filial, and reverent; yet instead one secretly deceives ruler and parents and does what is disloyal and unfilial.

This phrase ‘secretly deceive ruler and parents’ is spoken specifically of those who love reputation and of those who are affected and artificial in their feelings. The kindness of the state and of one’s parents toward us is like that of heaven and earth. If one draws a salary from the state yet neglects public business, or covets profit and perverts the law for private ends, or is treacherous and flattering, deceiving those above and hiding matters from those below, how could one let the ruler or head of state know such a mind? This is to deceive the ruler and head of state in secret! If one serves and provides for one’s parents without sincerity, is dishonest in handling affairs and in dealing with others, or covers over one’s own faults of disobedience toward one’s parents, how could one let one’s parents know such a mind? This is to deceive one’s parents in secret!

Emperor Xuanzong of the Ming dynasty was exceedingly fond of poetry, lyrics, and songs, and often commanded the ministers at court to compose matching pieces. There was a certain academician who thought his own talent very high, and each time he had finished composing a poem on imperial command, he would say: ‘The poem I have written is truly excellent! Not only can His Majesty not compose one like it, he cannot even understand its subtle points!’ Before long this academician, for having used in his poems characters that transgressed the temple name taboos of the imperial house and for words that touched upon mockery, was charged by the emperor with irreverence and stripped of his office.

In the period of the Three Kingdoms, in the state of Wu, there was a famous scholar named Gu Ti. Each time he received a letter from his father, he would read it kneeling, and moreover would answer aloud, phrase by phrase, the questions his father asked in the letter. And if his father were ill, Gu Ti would weep over his father’s letter, too grieved to speak a word. Again, Fan Xuan of the Jin dynasty, when he was eight years old, happened to injure his finger, and he cried aloud. Someone asked him: ‘Is it really as painful as that?’ Fan Xuan wept and said: ‘It is not because of the pain that I weep, but because my body, hair, and skin were received from my parents, and I dare not injure them; that is why I am grieved!’ Both of these gentlemen afterward held positions of the greatest honor and eminence.

In former times there were two brothers who took turns providing for their mother once every five days. The elder brother was rather poor, while the younger was better off. When it was the elder brother’s turn to provide for their mother, he was sometimes so poor that he could not even provide gruel; and once, during his five-day turn, because he lacked food for two days, he told his mother and asked her to stay for the time being at his younger brother’s house, promising that he would afterward make up those two days of provisions. When the mother heard this, she went to the younger brother’s house and told him the elder brother’s intent; but the younger brother had his wife hide the rice and firmly refused the elder brother’s arrangement. The mother was utterly helpless and returned to the elder brother’s house in tears; and at that moment thunder and lightning suddenly filled the sky, and there on the spot the younger brother and his wife were struck dead!

Toward teachers who transmit the Way, impart skills, and resolve doubts, one should reverently receive instruction; yet instead one treats them with disdain, truly failing greatly in the duty of a disciple in serving his teacher!

Our parents gave us our bodies, and it is only by the instruction of teachers that our learning can be brought to completion; therefore toward teachers and masters one should be as reverent as toward one’s ruler and one’s parents. When people today engage a teacher to educate their children, they often do no more than make a show of it, grudging their money and remiss in courtesy; and some even speak rudely and behave perversely, deliberately slighting the teacher, which makes them little different from birds and beasts! As for teachers themselves, their purpose is to open the wisdom of the younger generation, to make them conduct themselves well as human beings, and even to become sages and worthies; the hidden virtue of such spring-wind and nurturing-rain instruction is truly the greatest of all! How then can one accept another’s tuition and provisions, yet indulge their sons and younger brothers and not strictly manage and diligently teach them, so that they are in danger of never becoming useful; and some teachers even do the sons’ lessons in their place to deceive their fathers and elder brothers, or covet money and use bribes to buy rank and fame? The retribution for such offenses is beyond knowing how grave it is!

You Zuo and Yang Shi of the Song dynasty both became students under Cheng Yi. One day the two of them went together to pay their respects to their teacher, and it happened that Cheng Yi had closed his eyes and was sitting in meditation; so You Zuo and Yang Shi stood at their teacher’s side, waiting reverently, and waited a very long time. When Cheng Yi awoke, the snow outside the door had already piled more than a foot deep. Yet there was not the least look of weariness on the two men’s faces, and their propriety toward their teacher was all the more reverent and careful. Afterward both received the true transmission of their teacher’s learning, and together they spread the learning of Lian and Luo throughout the world.

Yue Fei of the Song dynasty had a teacher named Zhou Tong, who could draw a bow of three hundred catties. After Zhou Tong died, on the first and fifteenth of every month Yue Fei would surely prepare offerings and kneel and weep before his teacher’s grave; and he would shoot three arrows with the bow his teacher had given him before returning home.

In former times there was a farming household that had a son. The farmer’s desire to engage a teacher to teach his child to read well was most earnest; but his treatment of the child’s teacher went too far, for he did not understand the principle of revering the teacher. The food he gave the teacher was poor, nothing but unwholesome things; and the tuition he paid was very low. Though the teacher taught this child with all his heart and all his strength, and taught him for a long time, yet the child’s ability to read and understand essays written by others was passable, while when he came to write essays himself he was good for nothing at all. Strange indeed! In the end the child became a farmer like his father.
