The principle and the method of serving one’s teacher should be like that of a son or younger brother serving his father. When walking, one should follow behind the teacher; when sitting, one should sit beside the teacher’s seat; meeting the teacher on the road, one should stand up straight and salute him with folded hands; when the teacher speaks, one should listen with attentive ear and open mind. Even in the midst of calamity and grief, one must not change; whether in good fortune or ill, one should share the teacher’s sweet and bitter alike. While the teacher lives, one must not fail in the slightest degree in the propriety of serving him; and after the teacher has passed away, one should observe three years of mourning for him in the heart. One who can do all this may be reckoned to have fulfilled the propriety of a disciple serving his teacher and elders.

In former times there was a Teacher Wang who instructed and taught young children with the greatest devotion, and did not reckon the size of the tuition. And he often said to others: ‘Heaven, Earth, ruler, parents, and teacher, these five stand side by side! So once a child has bowed to me as his teacher, then his success or failure, his honor or disgrace for his whole life is my responsibility as his teacher! Therefore if a teacher cannot instruct his pupils with all his heart and all his strength, but instead leads them astray, then the offense is as grave as that of a quack physician who kills his patients!’ Teacher Wang also loved to tell children stories of filial piety and fraternal duty, saying: ‘One who seeks learning must first set his own mind and methods upright, and only then study letters and arts; he must first do well his own proper duties, and only then practice benevolence. For example, if a person is deficient in filial piety and fraternal duty, then though his talents cover the world, he is not worth taking seriously!’ In his later years Teacher Wang had a son, and this son was none other than Wenkang Gong; and everyone believed that this was the good reward for his teaching children well!

In recent times the Way of teachers has fallen lower and lower, until it has sunk to a point that makes one weep and lament aloud! Those who serve as models for others do not know, and never think about, the offenses of leading the young astray, which will surely bring the condemnation of the deities! In former times there was a scholar who, when he had passed sixty, said to his wife: ‘In this life of mine, though I have not prospered, I have been fortunate enough to obtain a very good teaching post, and only thereby have I been able to establish a household and a livelihood!’ Having said this, that night he had a dream in which he saw his father rebuke him, saying: ‘Your destiny was originally such that you might have passed the examinations and won rank and fame! It is only because you held a teaching post and could not teach with all your heart, and moreover was lazy and neglected your duties, that the Emperor of Literature has already struck your rank and fame from the register; and yet you do not know it, but are still there boasting and preening yourself!’ Alas! Seeing this example, we know that the offense of leading the young astray is truly most perilous!
Toward the superiors or masters whom one ought to serve, to fail in loyalty is betrayal!

The ‘service’ in ‘betraying those whom one serves’ refers to serving those above from below; for example, a subordinate serving a superior, a soldier serving a general, a servant or concubine serving a master, all are called service. And betrayal need not be open betrayal or defiance; so long as, when the one served is in urgent need, one cannot be his support, or at the critical moment of profit and loss one cannot show pity and relief, that is betrayal.

In the period of the Three Kingdoms, the famous general Lü Bu, brave and skillful in battle, at first bowed to Ding Yuan, the Inspector of Jingzhou, as his adoptive father, and Ding Yuan treated Lü Bu exactly as his own son. But Lü Bu was a man of courage without strategy, who forgot righteousness at the sight of profit. Coveting rank and wealth, and stirred up by his fellow townsman Li Su, he decided to throw in his lot with Dong Zhuo; and that very night Lü Bu took his knife and went into Ding Yuan’s tent, killed Ding Yuan, and cut off his head. The next day he brought Ding Yuan’s head and offered his service to Dong Zhuo, and moreover swore to bow to Dong Zhuo as his adoptive father. Later Lü Bu, for the sake of Diaochan and Minister of Education Wang Yun, thrust his halberd into his adoptive father Dong Zhuo and killed him. Not long after, Lü Bu was captured by Cao Cao’s army. Cao Cao had originally not intended to kill Lü Bu, and even wished to use him to help pacify the realm, so he asked Liu Bei’s opinion; but Liu Bei urged Cao Cao, saying: ‘My lord, have you not seen how Lü Bu served his adoptive fathers Ding Yuan and Dong Zhuo?’ When Cao Cao heard Liu Bei’s words, he found them quite reasonable, and ordered Lü Bu to be strangled.

Yang Zhong was the servant of Dai Xianke. Dai Xianke’s household was exceedingly wealthy, and he put Yang Zhong in charge of managing a farm for him. Yang Zhong managed it with great diligence, and the profits he obtained were considerable. Later, after Dai Xianke died, he left behind a son named Bojian, who was young and spent his days keeping company with bad youths, eating, drinking, and amusing himself; and in less than a few years he had squandered the entire family property, leaving only the farm that the servant Yang Zhong managed. Bojian then went to the farm to rely on Yang Zhong for his living; and Yang Zhong, having settled the farm’s accounts, handed everything over to Bojian to manage. Bojian was delighted, and once again squandered and spent money as before. Yang Zhong wept and urged Bojian not to waste money, but Bojian would not listen. One day the bad youths Bojian had formerly associated with came again to the house to gather with Bojian, and there they ate, drank, and gambled. Yang Zhong then came forward with a knife in his hand, and seizing the ringleader of the youths, said: ‘I, Yang Zhong, have served my master for more than thirty years. After my master died, the young master was young and knew nothing of the world, and you pack of foxes and dogs took the chance to lure him into doing wicked things. Now the Dai family property is entirely dissipated, and fortunately I have preserved this farm of my master’s; do you mean to waste and destroy the last remaining property of the Dai family as well? I shall now cut off your head first, and then go to the authorities and confess my crime and beg for death, to repay my master’s spirit in heaven!’ When these people heard this, they were convinced and submitted, and confessed their guilt to Yang Zhong, saying: ‘From this day on we shall never dare come to the Dai household again!’ Yang Zhong then brought out some cloth and gave it to them and sent them away; and then, weeping, he apologized to the young master Bojian, saying: ‘What your old servant has just done may have frightened the young master. I beg the young master from now on to change his old habit of wasting money and not to make friends with wicked companions again; only heed your old servant’s counsel, and your old servant will surely help the young master with all his heart and strength. In no more than two or three years, the Dai family estate can be restored and flourish again. Otherwise, your old servant will now throw himself into the sea and die; for your old servant truly cannot bear to see the young master starve in the future and bring utter shame upon the Dai family!’ When Bojian heard this, he felt deeply ashamed, and wept as he agreed. And sure enough, in only a few years Yang Zhong had restored all the fields and houses the Dai family had originally possessed; and afterward the old servant Yang Zhong lived to a great age, and in good health besides.
Toward the many ignorant people who do not understand reason, to speak falsehoods instead to deceive them, so that they believe what is false and come to harm.

Ignorant people are precisely the ones who ought to be guided according to the matter at hand, told how to distinguish good from evil and to understand principle, so that they may awaken and no longer be deluded and turned about. How can one deceive them because they are easy to deceive? The Shurangama Sutra says: ‘To display and delude those who are ignorant and do not understand reason, and to cause beings to doubt and go astray from their wisdom-life: such a person after death shall fall into the Interminable Hell and undergo measureless great suffering!’ Alas! Why should anyone take the trouble to create such offenses?

Mr. Liu Hefeng said: ‘In former times three people were traveling together, and when they came to a river they found it in flood, with the boat on the far bank. One of them was rather dull-witted, and the other two induced him to take off his clothes and swim across to bring the boat over. The simpleton really did as they said, took off his clothes and swam the river, and nearly drowned in the rushing water; but when he reached the far bank he poled the boat over and ferried his friends across. The two friends got on the boat, and the simpleton suddenly had a stomachache and needed to relieve himself, so he hurriedly got off the boat and went ashore to answer the call of nature; and the two friends at once waved their hands at him, saying: ‘Simpleton, it is growing dark, we cannot wait for you!’ And so they poled the boat across the river. Before long the river suddenly ran swift, the boat turned broadside and capsized, and both men drowned in the river; while the simpleton waited on the bank and came to no harm at all!’

In the Tang dynasty there was a man named Jiang Fu who came to the capital wearing a Daoist’s robes. Because no one knew him, he deceived people, saying: ‘I have already lived several hundred years, because I understand the secret of long life.’ Afterward Jiang Fu was summoned into the palace to serve Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, and moreover won the emperor’s favor and trust, so that his fame spread far and wide and was known to all. Later a certain imperial university student named Jing Yan went to pay his respects to Jiang Fu and asked him: ‘Sir, of what dynasty are you, exactly?’ Jiang Fu replied: ‘I am a man of the Liang dynasty.’ Jing Yan then asked: ‘Then have you ever held office?’ Jiang Fu said: ‘I once served as military commissioner of Liangzhou.’ When Jing Yan heard this he rebuked him, saying: ‘What sort of man are you, to dare be so audacious and false, deceiving the Son of Heaven and deluding the world? The Liang dynasty was in the south, beyond the Yangtze; how could there possibly be a Western Liangzhou? In the Liang dynasty there were only the offices of the four Pings, the four Ans, the four Zhengs, and the four Zhen generals; where did this title of military commissioner come from?’ When Jiang Fu heard this he gaped and could not answer, and felt exceedingly ashamed, with no place to hide himself; and within a few days he was dead.
Toward the many fellow students and friends, to slander them falsely instead and destroy their good name.
Fellow students and friends are as close in affection as brothers; moreover, friends are one of the five relationships. How can one slander them falsely, with a belly full of spears and lances?

The Buddha said: ‘In the relations between friends, each has five duties to fulfill. First, if either has done evil, they should admonish each other and forbid the doing of evil again. Second, if either falls ill, they should visit, care for, and nurse each other. Third, if either learns of the other’s private matters, he must not speak of them to outsiders. Fourth, they should respect and praise each other, not break off their association, and not bear grudges. Fifth, if their wealth is unequal, they should support and help each other, and must not slander one another.’

Someone may ask: ‘After associating with a friend, one discovers that he is not good, and wishes to break off the friendship, yet fears to wound the affection between us; but not to break it off is to harbor resentment while associating with him as a friend.’ Zhu Xi replied: ‘That is not harboring resentment while associating with a friend; it is to store resentment in the heart while outwardly associating with him as a friend, and that is what harboring resentment means! If a friend is not good, then by affection and right one ought naturally to keep some distance from him; but one should also distance oneself gradually. If he has no very grave fault, why must one shut him out a thousand li away? And moreover, if one only keeps applying a most sincere heart without cease, one can surely transform him and bring him to awakening! This is what is meant by saying that relatives should not lose the principle of being relatives, and friends should not lose the principle of being friends.’

Wang Yangming of the Ming dynasty said: ‘In the relations between friends, humility and an open mind are of the greatest importance! When friends meet, each should be modest and yielding, and reverently accommodate the other. Broadly speaking, there should be few occasions of admonition, reproof, and fault-finding, and many occasions of earnest guidance, praise, and encouragement!’

Mr. Wen Jiexiao said: “In making friends, one should appreciate the other’s strong points and not dwell on his weak ones. With a friend of upright and unbending character, bear with his fierce temper; with a friend of free and easy disposition, bear with his scattered ways; with a friend simple and honest, bear with his dull heaviness; with a friend light-hearted and open, bear with his levity. In this way you will gain countless benefits, and this too is the very best way to make friends!”

Mr. Zhang Qianzai of the Song dynasty, whose style name was Yi’e, was a close friend of Wen Tianxiang. When Wen Tianxiang was prime minister, at the height of his eminence and prosperity, he time and again recommended Zhang Qianzai to the court and earnestly invited him to take office, but Zhang Qianzai refused every time. Later, when Wen Tianxiang was defeated in battle against the Mongol armies, he was taken back to Jizhou under guard and imprisoned; Zhang Qianzai then secretly made his way into the prison to visit him, saying: “If you, my lord prime minister, are sent to the north, I too will go north with you.” When Zhang Qianzai reached the north, he took up lodging near the prison where Wen Tianxiang was held; and for the three years Wen Tianxiang lay in that cell, Zhang Qianzai provided for him for three years, so that Wen Tianxiang never felt any want in his daily life. Later, when the Yuan court ordered Wen Tianxiang put to death, Zhang Qianzai hid his head away carefully in a wooden box; and afterwards, on inquiring, he learned that Wen Tianxiang’s wife, Lady Ouyang, had died among the captives, so he cremated her body, gathered up her bones, and placed them in a bag. Then Zhang Qianzai carried the wooden box and the bag southward; when he reached Wen Tianxiang’s home village, he gave them to his descendants for burial. On the very night before Zhang Qianzai arrived, Wen Tianxiang’s son dreamed that his father said to him: “I have come back together with Uncle Zhang!” And sure enough, the next day Zhang Qianzai arrived at the Wen household.

Hence people of later ages had a saying to describe a friendship that holds through life and death: “A friendship of life and death: a thousand years, one osprey.” This saying is exactly so, with not the slightest exaggeration! Mr. Shen Zhonghua said: “To fail a friend who has died is to injure the Way of friendship even more gravely than to fail a friend who still lives!” Now when we make friends, let us ask ourselves: can we hold fast through life and death without ever letting our hearts change?

Guo Zhi of the Song dynasty composed fu with uncommon excellence, and thereby won considerable fame. His fellow student Li Mian, however, envied his talent and reputation and slandered him. As a result, Li Mian failed to pass the examinations several times in succession. Later Guo Zhi was the first to pass the imperial examination, and then went on to pass the provincial examination as well, while only then did Li Mian barely qualify for selection in the Illustrious Classics examination. On the day the results were posted, Li Mian felt deeply ashamed and regretful, and resolved to return home and never sit for the examinations again. When Guo Zhi heard the news, he set out at once in pursuit, caught up with Li Mian, and brought him back; only afterwards did Li Mian pass.
From this we can see that when a man slanders another, the other suffers no harm whatever on that account; the slanderer only makes himself mean and harsh, and brings retribution upon himself!
To use falsehood, false accusation, deception, and hypocrisy of every kind as means to censure and attack the private affairs and faults of others.

To speak without any basis is called falsehood; to slander wantonly is called false accusation; to delude others by cunning schemes is called deception; to disguise one’s true feelings and deceive the world is called hypocrisy. Taken separately, these four make four kinds; taken together, they are simply dishonesty. Know that “sincerity is the Way of Heaven; to think of sincerity is the Way of man.” Now if a man casts aside sincerity and instead uses falsehood, false accusation, deception, and hypocrisy, is he not rebelling against the Way of Heaven and losing the Way of man? Such a mind is exceedingly bad, and such conduct is exceedingly dangerous. A man of this kind is one marked out for the thinnest fortune under heaven. So if such a person does not fall into the three evil paths of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell, where else will he fall? In the Qing dynasty, Mr. Sun Tingquan of Yidu was by nature utterly simple and sincere, with no scheming in him at all, and so the Shunzhi Emperor often called him Honest Sun. Each time a vacancy arose among the ministers of the various ministries, the emperor would always say: “Let us use Honest Sun after all!” Three times in succession he said this, and Honest Sun became prime minister! So how could an honest and generous nature ever ruin a man?

There was a man named Xue Fu who made his living by inventing and fabricating legal plaints for others to bring to court; he could turn a case without merit into a case with merit, and by such tricks he grew rich. Later he felt uneasy in his heart, and so he set up a Daoist altar of offering and repented of his sins before Heaven. After the Daoist priest had performed his rites, he rose from prostration before the altar and said: “The Jade Emperor has handed down his judgment: the house of Xue Fu is to be given over to the fire god to deal with, and Xue Fu himself is to be given over to the water god to deal with.” In time Xue Fu’s house was indeed burned to the ground by a great fire, and Xue Fu himself fell into the water and drowned.

In the period of the Five Dynasties, a misunderstanding and conflict arose between two officials of the kingdom of Min, Xue Wenjie and Wu Ying. It happened that the king of Min, Wang Lin, had sent a shaman into the palace to see whether any ghosts were haunting it. Xue Wenjie seized the chance and first said to Wu Ying: “The emperor suspects you of commanding both high office and great power; at this time you should plead illness and ask for leave to rest at home. If the emperor sends an envoy to inquire after you, you should pretend to have a headache when you answer him. I can put in a good word for you before the emperor.” Having heard him out, Wu Ying agreed to do so. Xue Wenjie then told the shaman: “Wu Ying intends to rebel; the Jade Emperor has driven a copper nail into Wu Ying’s head, and that is why he suffers from headaches!” The emperor sent an envoy to investigate the matter and find out whether it was true or false, and Wu Ying did indeed tell the envoy that he suffered from headaches. Thereupon the king of Min sent men to put Wu Ying to death. Wu Ying died because of Xue Wenjie’s false accusation, and the common people felt bitter hatred over it. It happened that the king of Min then ordered troops to be sent to resist an invasion by the kingdom of Wu, but the army refused to advance, declaring that it would march only if Xue Wenjie were handed over. The king of Min had no choice but to have Xue Wenjie bound and placed in the cangue and delivered to the army; and there the officers and men at once cut all the flesh from his body with their knives, in a single instant.

In the Song dynasty, an official named Zhao Tingchen, using deceitful schemes, made an agreement with the Dongrong tribes beyond the mountain passes to surrender to the court; then, after plying the would-be surrendering Dongrong people with drink until they were drunk, he killed them all. He even spread the word that the Dongrong were plotting rebellion, and took credit for quelling the matter as his own merit. Through this Zhao Tingchen was vigorously promoted by the court and rose to a prominent office. Later he dreamed of a Dongrong man whom he had killed, who said to him: 'I have come to repay you for the deceit you used against us Dongrong people!' Not long afterward, Zhao Tingchen had a son who passed the examinations at a young age and became an official; but then this son suddenly, for no reason, went mad and rebelled, breaking the laws of the realm. Zhao Tingchen and his wife, implicated by their son, were punished by the court and exiled beyond the passes, where they were finally killed by the Dongrong people.

In the Song dynasty, the treacherous minister Ding Wei, when dealing with others, never spoke the truth; he even said: 'If a person's heart is sincere and honest, then he can accomplish nothing at all; he will merely be bullied by others!' With such a mind as Ding Wei's, it is no wonder no one knew what schemes he was concocting in his heart, which no one could fathom. At the time, all the people under heaven regarded Ding Wei as one of the five ghosts. To be sure, Ding Wei's falsehood, deceit, and hypocrisy were worse than any ghost's; and of course his final end was too disgraceful to mention.
To expose the private affairs or faults of one's clan and relatives, and attack them for these.

Relatives of the same surname are called clan; relatives of a different surname are called kin. Though ties of relation differ in closeness and distance, all of them are persons I should care for. I ought to treat them with affection and sincerity; when they meet calamity I should share it with them; when they meet hardship and want, I should promptly aid them; I should cover up their family shame and together resist outside insult. How could we struggle against one another, quibbling over the smallest matter to the last penny, or even undermine and attack each other, waiting for the chance to denounce and take revenge? As the saying goes: 'To break a branch wounds the tree's heart; to cut off the root severs the tree's pulse.' This is a saying worthy of vigilance for everyone.

In the Spring and Autumn period, Yan Pingzhong, the minister of Qi, lived in great frugality. Duke Jing of Qi thought he was concealing the rewards the ruler had bestowed on him, and so asked him about it. Yanzi answered Duke Jing: 'Since your servant received Your Majesty's favor, being raised to honor, the people of my father's clan have all ridden in carriages; the people of my mother's clan have all had ample clothing and food; and the people of my wife's clan no longer suffer any to die of hunger or cold. Further, there are more than three hundred scholars of Qi who wait upon your servant for their food and drink. In acting this way, has your servant concealed Your Majesty's rewards to me, or has he displayed them?'

Yanzi distributed the king of Qi's rewards with the people of his father's clan given first priority, those of his mother's clan second, those of his wife's clan third, and only finally extending to those of more distant relations. This is what the ancients meant when they said: 'Extend one's love to those one loves, and on to those one does not love.' Yanzi can be counted as a person skilled at fostering harmony among his clan and relatives! If everyone had a heart like Yanzi's and could well harmonize with their kin, then in this world there would be no such heartless, unrighteous events as attacking one's own clan.
A person of rigid constitution and fiery temperament cannot be kind, gentle, and generous in his dealings with others.

The perseverance that Confucius praised was because of a will firm and upright and one that abides by principle; whereas the rigidity that Taishang warns against is because of a person who is easily given to anger. Traditional medicine calls the condition of paralysis 'benevolence-less' (bu ren), precisely because this ailment knows neither pain nor itch. A person given to forceful anger, in dealing with others, likewise knows neither pain nor itch; he bears an aura of killing intent, which is what the proverb calls an iron heart and stone bowels. How can such a person be benevolent? Yet in the end, rigidity is never not shattered and broken! If, after suffering several great losses, a person gradually transforms toward gentleness, that is his great good fortune.

In the Song dynasty, Bao Zheng, whom the common people called Bao Qingtian (Bao the Clear Sky), served as magistrate of Kaifeng Prefecture. His nature was firm and unbending. When his subordinates reported matters to him that were not reasonable, he refuted them to their faces; if what they said was sound, he would accept it with a gentle countenance and correct himself. For this everyone greatly admired him. One should know that to be firm and yet principled, and decisive when encountering affairs, this is the courage of the benevolent!

In the Song dynasty, Zhang Ruqing, when he served as circuit judge, whenever he interrogated criminals would apply every kind of punishment to the offender once, regardless of whether the crime was light or heavy; and he called this 'beating a full set.' The prisoners being interrogated called Zhang Ruqing 'Yama come to summon.' Later, after his term as circuit judge was complete, he returned to his hometown. On the night the boat he was on stopped at Gaoyou, he dreamed of several hundred people with broken heads and broken legs surrounding him, demanding his life. After returning home, Zhang Ruqing actually saw a fierce ghost in broad daylight, and died with blood flowing from his seven orifices.

That those who are rigid and cruel do not die a good death is a truth that need not be repeated; yet after they die, they fall into the three evil paths, and who knows how long a time must pass before they can escape! So when one sees Zhang Ruqing's example, and reflects further on the retribution he received after death, then all who are rigid and cruel ought also to wake up!
A nature fierce and cruel, and fond of willfulness, acting on one's own opinion and believing oneself always right.

Whenever a wise person does something, he knows how to make use of others; whereas a person without wisdom relies entirely on himself. One should realize that for a foolish person to act on his own is already unacceptable, let alone for one who is fierce, cruel, and self-willed, which is even worse!

The Buddha said: 'A fierce and cruel person is like a vicious, bad horse, difficult to tame. If a person is fierce and cruel, he easily clings to his own views, believes himself right, and refuses to yield to others. For this reason no beneficial friends or good teachers come near him, and no one is willing to tell him the great principles of conducting himself and dealing with the world. Thus, of the causes of a person's committing evil and drawing resentment upon himself, there is none more serious than this.'

Wang Anshi was prime minister under Emperor Shenzong of Song. In his conduct he was fond of suspicion, jealousy, and self-willed obstinacy; he pushed aside the loyal and good, cheated the world to steal a reputation; and even, with boundless audacity, slandered the sages and worthies, going so far as to have the brass to claim sagehood for himself. His administration ruined the realm's talent; his scholarship corrupted the hearts of society. His New Meanings of the Three Classics and his Explanation of Characters slandered and reviled the sages, and shattered and crushed the great Way; and this was not all. For example, because the Spring and Autumn Annals can correct the proper names of ruler and minister and fix the praise and blame of persons, so that rebels and traitors are filled with fear, Wang Anshi told scholars not to study the Spring and Autumn Annals. The Records of the Grand Historian and the Book of Han record the facts and principles of a dynasty's rise and fall, safety and peril, survival and ruin, order and disorder, and can serve as a mirror for later generations; yet Wang Anshi told scholars not to read the Records and the Book of Han. The great writer of the Han dynasty, Yang Xiong, when Wang Mang usurped the Han, failed to keep the integrity of a subject and could not give his life for the state; he even wrote an essay attacking the tyranny of Qin while praising the founding of the new dynasty. Wang Anshi actually said: 'Yang Xiong's conduct accords with what Confucius said in the Analects: nothing may and nothing may not.' (In fact it is exactly the opposite.) And Feng Dao held office through four dynasties and eight rulers, yet Wang Anshi said: 'Feng Dao is truly a man skilled at avoiding calamity and knowing how to preserve himself.' If all the ministers of the court had listened to Wang Anshi's words and learned his way of being a person, then there would be no loyal, righteous, and principled ministers left in the court!

When Wang Anshi first became prime minister, he was still able to get along harmoniously with the worthy gentlemen of the court. Later, because of the new laws he promoted, with which the worthy gentlemen of the court could not agree, quarrels arose, and Wang Anshi excluded them, even demoting them and exiling them to far places. His son Wang Pang even went so far as to say: 'Once we cut off the heads of Han Qi and Fu Bi, the new laws will be smoothly implemented,' and as for the rest, there is no need to speak. Afterward, because those who attacked Wang Anshi's new laws grew more numerous, his words and actions became even more arrogant, fierce, unrestrained, and strange. He even said such wild words as: 'Heaven's changes are not to be feared, the words of men are not to be heeded, and the laws of the ancestors are not to be kept.' At this point his offense was deep and heavy, reaching the fullness of evil. His only son, Wang Pang, suddenly developed a virulent sore on his back and died young. Wang Anshi was deeply grieved, and petitioned Shenzong, pleading illness, to resign the post of prime minister. Later Shenzong also came to dislike Wang Anshi and removed him from the post. At this time Wang Anshi had lost the emperor's trust, grieved for his only son's early death and the loss of an heir, and his own cruelty and inhumanity, his perverse course of action, had drawn the hatred and curses of the people. The worthy gentlemen he had once excluded and exiled also successively came to power and abolished the new laws he had advocated and carried out. Wang Anshi was thereby filled with shame, and died in fright and terror.
[Explanation] For a wicked person who does evil, to say he is right; and for a good person who does good, to say he is wrong. Such a determination of right and wrong is far too improper!

A truly virtuous and benevolent gentleman possesses sufficient wisdom to distinguish good and evil and to judge right and wrong properly. One should know that right and wrong, for a single person, concern that person's good or evil; for a township, they concern the township's benefit or harm; for the world and the state, they concern the safety or peril of the world and the state. So how could one fail to be cautious and careful! If one judges right and wrong lightly and improperly, at one's own whim, that is far too dangerous!

In the Song dynasty, Yin Shilu, whether in conducting himself toward others or in teaching his students, was perfectly clear between right and wrong, never in the least careless. Before his death, he personally wrote a letter of farewell to Fan Zhongyan. When Fan Zhongyan received the letter, he hurried at once to Yin Shilu's home; by then Yin Shilu had already bathed, changed his clothes, and was sitting upright, having passed away. When Fan Zhongyan saw that Yin Shilu had died, he wept bitterly. Unexpectedly, Yin Shilu opened his eyes and said to Fan Zhongyan: 'Have I not already written to bid you farewell? You need not have come to see me again. Does not the principle that all things born must die, do you not know it?' When Yin Shilu finished speaking, he made a bow of farewell to Fan Zhongyan and passed away.

From this we can know that if Yin Shilu's learning and virtue had not already been cultivated to the perfect maturity, how could he, at that perilous moment between life and death, a critical instant, have had such steadiness of concentration, able even when disturbed to respond calmly without confusion? Therefore, in entering the Way one must surely use both knowledge and practice together, and 'knowledge' is especially important; this is the reason.

In the Song dynasty, when Cai Jing was prime minister, he designated the worthy gentlemen Sima Guang, Su Dongpo, Cheng Yi, Wang Xianke, and others, one hundred and twenty in all, as a 'treacherous faction.' He further memorialized the emperor for approval to carve the names of the 'treacherous faction' on a great stele at the Duanli gate, and ordered all the prefectures and counties in the land to do likewise. The common people felt this was greatly unfair. Before long, this stele was shattered by lightning, and Cai Jing, his plot having failed, was demoted, banished, and died in exile.

For a wicked person, one should keep far from him, yet instead one turns one's heart toward him; for a good person, one should draw near him, yet instead one turns against him. Such turning toward and away is truly inappropriate!

'Toward' is what one should incline to; for example, good persons and good deeds are what we should incline toward. 'Away' is what one should turn from; for example, wicked persons and wicked deeds are what we should turn from. If one turns toward the wicked and away from the upright, this is called a perverse turning toward and away. If one fails to notice for even a moment and the turning toward and away loses its propriety, it will lead to the ruin of one's name and person for life. Therefore, in turning toward and away, one must be especially cautious and careful!

In the Tang dynasty, Song Shenxi was prime minister under Emperor Wenzong. Because Zheng Zhu had seized power greatly, Song Shenxi wished to remove him; he had his friend Wang Fan appointed governor of Jingzhao, and secretly instructed Wang Fan to investigate Zheng Zhu's unlawful conduct. But Wang Fan, because Zheng Zhu had once promoted him, told Zheng Zhu of Song Shenxi's scheme. Zheng Zhu was thereby greatly frightened, and struck first, instead slandering Prime Minister Song Shenxi as plotting treason. Song Shenxi was demoted and exiled to Kaizhou as adjutant, and in his resentment died. Later, Lady Song dreamed that Song Shenxi led her to a pit outside the capital, in which there were several executed prisoners. Song Shenxi then lifted up one dead prisoner to show his wife, and said: 'This dead prisoner is Wang Fan; I have already petitioned the Lord on High!' Because Song Shenxi was furious and shouted loudly, Lady Song woke from her dream; she then silently fixed the dream in her heart. Before long, Li Xun and Zheng Zhu plotted together to kill the eunuchs; they memorialized the emperor to order the eunuchs to gather at the imperial army camp to view the auspicious dew at dawn, and then dispatched Wang Fan and others to lead troops to kill the eunuchs. Wang Fan was so frightened his legs trembled and he dared not go; the affair consequently failed, and Wang Fan was cut in half at the waist. Several others were killed together and were all buried in the same pit outside the city.

In the Song dynasty, the worthy minister Liu Zhi once discussed the ten harms of the new corvée and labor laws that Wang Anshi had implemented. Wang Anshi reproached Liu Zhi for his perverse turning toward and away, and reported him to the emperor, who issued an edict ordering Liu Zhi to analyze the reasons he opposed the new laws. Liu Zhi then reported to the emperor: 'What your servant turns toward is loyalty and uprightness; what he turns from is evil and flattery. What he turns toward is righteousness; what he turns from is profit. What he turns toward is the sovereign and father; what he turns from is the powerful traitor. If your servant is punished for this, it is what he deserves; but the new laws that Wang Anshi has implemented will in the end harm the people of the world! I beg Your Majesty not to forget what I have said!' Liu Zhi actually dared to speak the truth before the emperor, and everyone sweated for him; but Liu Zhi held that what should be said must be said, and what should be done must be done, and that one must not be timid for the sake of one's own interest. Later Liu Zhi became prime minister.

Master Lu said: 'To turn toward what one should turn toward is not done out of selfish motives; and to turn away from what one should turn away from is also for the public good, for the world, the state, and the people, and never has calculated personal fortune or misfortune. Yet fortune and misfortune come precisely from this; and this too is a warning for those who are unwilling to be a Liu Zhi and are content to be a Wang Fan!'
There are officials who actually dare to carry out tyrannical government, oppressing the people, in order to greedily seize merit and reward.

A candle meeting the night accomplishes the merit of dispelling darkness; a boat receiving the buoyancy of water accomplishes the merit of carrying goods. In general, once the water flows and the channel forms, merit naturally reveals itself; there is no need at all to seize merit! So once one has the intention to seize merit, then a general may let his army plunder and kill, an official may arbitrarily increase grain taxes and labor corvée, and a judge may aggravate the punishment of offenders, all without concern and done at will. Yet these are all acts of exchanging the people's flesh and blood for personal merit and fame. Even if the merit is obtained, it is only a promotion; but disaster follows right after, and it is not only the calamity of losing one's life! Though a person be ever so foolish, he should not go that far. Let us look at the ancients. For example, the great Song general Cao Bin, when he took Jiangnan, did not kill a single person! The Han dynasty's Ji An, in order to relieve a famine, forged an imperial edict and opened the granary, saving tens of thousands of starving people! And the Han dynasty's Yu Dingguo, when serving as commandant of justice trying cases, the people, even when convicted, did not feel they had been wronged! For their time, were they not the greatest meritorious servants of the state!

In the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, because of a luxurious life, the expenses of the palace grew ever greater and the funds were insufficient; Xuanzong was unwilling to transfer funds from elsewhere. At this time Wang Hong, a director of the Ministry of Revenue

, knowing the emperor's intent, then increased taxes, adding to the burden of the people's levies, collecting extra tax money each year amounting to as much as tens of millions, stored in the treasury for the emperor's use. The emperor therefore thought Wang Hong truly capable and able to enrich the state, and specially promoted him to the post of inspecting commissioner of the capital area; before long he was further promoted to vice minister of revenue and governor of Jingzhao. Yet officials inside and outside the court, and the common people, all sighed in resentment over Wang Hong's conduct. Before long Wang Hong, implicated by a grave crime of his younger brother, was ordered by the emperor to die.

In the Song dynasty, Wang Shao proposed that the emperor open up Xihe, and thereby killed quite a number of people, accumulating merit to rise to the post of commissioner of military affairs. He also deliberately killed the Qiang people who had surrendered to Song, cutting off the heads of old and young alike; and he even found ways to let his fellow townsmen claim credit for accomplishments and gain office and rank. In his later years Wang Shao deeply regretted this matter, and asked many elder monks about the principle of cause and effect. The elders all said: 'To kill under the king's law is like a boat passing over and crushing snails and clams; naturally it is an unintentional fault!' Only Diao Jingchun said: 'I fear only that you cannot overcome your own heart. If you can overcome it, then naturally you would not be asking this question.' After hearing this, Wang Shao's heart was filled with even greater fear. Later a virulent sore grew on his back, and he often cried out: 'I see many people with broken heads and broken feet coming to demand my life!' In the end his chest broke open with a great hole and he died; his eldest son spat blood and died; another son was beheaded for breaking the law, and Wang Shao's whole family was wiped out.
To flatter a superior official, catering to his wishes.

When a superior official has not yet made a decision, there is still opportunity to advise him and turn him back; but if at that moment someone flatters the official, then the official's resolve becomes all the more firm, to the point that it can no longer be advised back. This is not only the case of a minister toward a ruler; for example, a subordinate official catering to his superior, a local gentryman catering to the government office, a staff member catering to his manager, a servant catering to his master; all these are such cases. In general, whoever occupies a superior position should in every matter act according to principle, and must not be covetous and selfish, giving others an opening to flatter and fawn on him. And those in lower positions, how can they seek unrighteous merit and fame, or covet unrighteous wealth? One should know that flattery and catering, bending the knee in fawning, only vainly causes one to lose one's conscience and character, and to form endless karmic enmity with others!

In the Xuande era of the Ming dynasty, the court dispatched the eunuch Wang Sanbao with ships to the barbarous nations of the Western Ocean to seek rare treasures of the age. In the Tianshun era, someone again advised the emperor to dispatch ships southward to the Western Ocean once more; the court ordered the Ministry of War to bring out the archives of the previous voyage, preparing to plan sending another expedition. At the time Xiang Zhong was in charge of the Ministry of War and ordered his subordinate to bring out the archives for review; Liu Daxia, then a director of the Ministry of War, upon learning the news, first went to the storeroom and hid the archives, so that the officials ordered to review them searched the storeroom for half the day and found nothing; and because the archives could not be found, the proposal gradually came to nothing. But Xiang Zhong reproached his subordinates, saying: 'The archives were clearly placed in the storeroom; how could they be missing?' Liu Daxia then said with a smile: 'On the previous voyage to the Western Ocean, the money and grain expended reached as high as hundreds of thousands, and the soldiers and people killed or injured could not be counted. Even if treasures were obtained, they would do the state no good! This was a bad affair, and ministers should rather have dissuaded the emperor from it. If the old archives still exist, they should also be destroyed to remove the future harm; how can we be pressing about whether the archives exist at all?' When Xiang Zhong heard Liu Daxia's words, he immediately apologized to Liu Daxia, saying: 'My knowledge is shallow and I could not think of such a profound principle; today, from what you have raised, one might say your hidden virtue moved Heaven, and this position of mine should belong to you!' Later Liu Daxia indeed became minister of war.

Emperor Taizong of Tang once pointed at a tree and said: 'This tree truly is a fine tree!' From then on Yuwen Shiji ceaselessly praised the tree to everyone he met. When Taizong learned of this, he said sternly to Yuwen Shiji: 'Wei Zheng has long urged me to keep far from fawning, flattering sycophants, and I never knew what a sycophant looked like; today I finally know, so you are the sycophant!' When Yuwen Shiji heard this, he immediately bowed his head and confessed his fault to the emperor, filled with shame!

Guo Chongtao, a minister of the Later Tang of the Five Dynasties, in order to cater to the wishes of Emperor Zhuangzong, urged him to install Lady Liu as empress; but Guo Chongtao's motive in urging the installation of Lady Liu was to form a connection with her. Yet later it was Lady Liu who spoke ill of Guo Chongtao before the emperor, causing him to be killed. Alas! At first Guo Chongtao, to cater to Zhuangzong's wishes, urged the installation of Lady Liu, precisely wishing to secure his own position; yet he thereby instead brought down a grim disaster on himself. So of what use are flattery and catering?
To receive kindness from another and not only fail to think of gratitude and return, but even be ungrateful and treacherous.

People of old, even when receiving the kindness of a single meal given by another, would surely repay it; even if unable to repay, they would surely hold it in grateful remembrance, never daring to forget it for a moment. The Great Treatise of Wisdom says: 'To receive another's kindness and not know to repay it with gratitude, such a person is worse than an animal!' These words are truly fitting! Yet among kindnesses, there are the so-called great kindnesses of four kinds: first, the great kindness of Heaven and Earth; second, the great kindness of one's parents; third, the great kindness of the state; and fourth, the great kindness of one's teachers. Some people muddle through a whole lifetime, never at all repaying these four great kindnesses, yet preen themselves over repaying private favors and small kindnesses. This is what is meant by casting away the root to pursue the branches, and is not true repayment of kindness!

In the Tang dynasty, Shi Wuwei and Zhang Congzhen were good friends. Shi Wuwei's family was very poor, and Zhang Congzhen often helped and supported him, so that his family lacked nothing in clothing and food, and gave him money to engage in trade; within a few years Shi Wuwei became wealthy. Then Zhang Congzhen's home caught fire, and his family property was all burned up. Zhang Congzhen, having no way out, went to visit and ask Shi Wuwei for help; but Shi Wuwei was ungrateful, and would not even regard Zhang Congzhen. At that moment Zhang Congzhen was filled with emotion, and could only sigh to Heaven in vain

sighing in helplessness. At that moment, all of a sudden, dark clouds gathered in the sky and thunder and lightning flashed together; after Shi Wuwei was struck by lightning, he actually turned into a cow, and on the belly of this cow there appeared several great red characters: 'The ungrateful Shi Wuwei.' After ten days, this cow also died.

As the saying goes: 'Even animals know to repay kindness!' For example, the horse lowered its rein, the dog spread the grass; the little snake, to repay the Marquis of Sui for saving its life, carried two pearls in its mouth and presented them to him; and the yellow sparrow carried a jade ring in its beak to repay Yang Bao for saving its life. If animals are this mindful of repaying kindness, how can a person dare to violate moral principle and the Way of Heaven; does he not fear turning into a cow as Shi Wuwei did?
Toward those one bears a grudge, not to think of meeting resentment with virtue, but to harbor hatred and revenge, and to keep it always in mind, refusing to let it rest!

As for the great hatred of killing one's ruler or father, and the resentment of being separated from one's own flesh and blood, a gentleman naturally has his way of meeting such hatred with uprightness. As for private enmities and small grudges, one can dispel them by reason and forgive them by fellow-feeling, and in this way private enmity and small grudge can be dissolved. If one still keeps them always in mind, then one resentment repaid by another goes on unceasingly forever!

In the Tang dynasty, Li Deyu, when he was prime minister, formed no few enmities with many people. Later Li Deyu was demoted and exiled to Zhuyai (present-day Hainan Island). Once at Zhuyai he saw hung on the wall of a Buddhist temple more than ten gourds, and felt this was very strange; so he asked the monk of the temple. The monk told Li Deyu: 'These are all the ashes of people! These people, because they offended the powerful prime minister Li Deyu, were demoted and exiled to Zhuyai, and died here. This old monk, seeing that they died in a foreign land and their bodies were left unburied, felt it was too pitiful; so he pitied and sympathized with them, cremated their remains, and placed them in gourds, awaiting their descendants to come and take them home.' When Li Deyu heard the old monk say this, he was so frightened that he staggered backward, his heart ached as if wrung, and he ached until he died.

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: 'When others use their power against me, I use a broad and generous measure to tolerate their deviant conduct; in this way I can sweep away the clouds that layer by layer obstruct the heart, and extinguish the kindling spark of revenge in the mind.' Therefore a gentleman does not dwell on past wrongs!
